## Current Status & History

**Family History:**
Emma Rose Callahan has a reported family history of ADHD. Her complex background includes early trauma prior to adoption and a history of multiple placements, as documented in her educational and clinical records. The family is aware of her diagnoses of Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD) and ADHD, and her current caregivers have been actively involved in supporting her developmental progress since adoption.

**Birth and Developmental History:**
Emma Rose Callahan was adopted at 19 months, so detailed information about her birth circumstances is limited. Available records indicate a birth weight of 6 pounds 4 ounces and that she was born in Hollister, California. There is evidence of alleged in utero exposure to methamphetamines and severe neglect during infancy, which may have contributed to her early developmental challenges. Historical assessments note suspected delays in overall cognitive development and exposure to trauma, including neglect.

Emma Rose experienced delays in walking, taking her first steps at around 19 months, and began talking at approximately age 2. She started using sentences as early as age 3. Overall, she met most developmental milestones on time except for these delays, and she has progressed developmentally since being in the care of her adoptive parents. Early records also document delays in speech and language, but more recent school reports indicate age-appropriate communication and motor skills. Emma Rose participates in physical education with peers and her handwriting is noted as legible, falling within expected boundaries. By age 3, she was toilet-trained during the day, although she experienced frequent accidents at that age.

**Health History:**
Emma Rose Callahan has several medical diagnoses and a history of medication management. She is diagnosed with hypothyroidism and is currently adjusting the dosage of her medication. Her prescribed medications include Geodon, Trileptal, and Vyvance, and previous regimens have involved guanfacine, Singular, and melatonin at night. Emma Rose has no known allergies but experiences seasonal allergies.

She has had a few procedures, including an appendectomy in April 2019, which according to her own report, has not resulted in ongoing issues. She also reported having her tonsils removed, which resolved her sleep apnea. At the start of the current school year, Emma Rose was regularly falling asleep in class, particularly in the morning. She is being fitted for a CPAP machine and will participate in a sleep study over the summer. Her mother also reports ongoing sleep problems and sensitivity to noise and touch. School and medical records confirm that Emma Rose is not blind or visually impaired, nor deaf or hard of hearing. Current school records indicate that no health plan is required at present, although her mother will notify the school if circumstances change.

## Educational History

**School History:**
[SCHOOL HISTORY CHART — server-owned; do not generate cells]

**School Experience:**
Emma Rose Callahan began her formal education at Sunshine Bilingual Chinese/English preschool and Bright Start Preschool, both bilingual programs, following her adoption by her current family at age 19 months. She later attended Creekside Oaks and Oak Meadow School as her schools of attendance, and was subsequently enrolled by her parents in a private school. In fourth grade, Emma Rose’s academic functioning was within the below average to average range compared to grade peers, with noted strengths in early reading skills, oral reading fluency, reading comprehension, spelling, essay composition, alphabet writing fluency, and numerical operations. Math problem solving and fluency in addition and subtraction, as well as multi-step word problems, were areas of below average performance and inconsistency while multiplication fluency showed relative strength. Her reading fluency improved from 52 correct words per minute to 85 CWPM over the course of fourth grade, with comprehension progressing from 71% to 75% accuracy.

Emma’s written expression demonstrated strengths in essay composition, although she often formulated responses containing fragmented or run-on sentences with errors in subject/verb agreement, capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. She could write opinion pieces with closure, achieving accuracy targets with fewer than six to eight errors in most opportunities.

Currently, Emma Rose is a ninth grader at Ridgeway High School, participating in the Ridgeway-Cordova SELPA. She entered FHS with SAI English and Study Skills and attends Ridgeway High School, currently with good attendance and the ability to follow directions. Diagnostic assessment places her reading at a seventh-grade level and a diagnostic score of 989 at the 18th national percentile. Her performance in literature and informational text is consistent (8/15 each), with scores in language and vocabulary slightly below (5/14), and she earned 15/25 on her recent vocabulary quiz. Her math academic profile shows persistent areas of weakness in math fluency, numerical operations, and multi-step reasoning, with subtest scores reflecting challenges in algebra, fractions, geometry, measurement, and operations. She has demonstrated growth in math through assessments, including an 86% score on her last summative assessment.

Emma Rose continues to develop her writing, working on two-paragraph expository essays with an emerging topic sentence and supporting details. Her accuracy was at 75% as of May 2024 and she is able to use metaphors in her writing. She appreciates listening to improve her verbal expression and expresses interest in public speaking. While she shows confidence in English and writing, she reports not liking math.

**Intervention:**
Emma Rose Callahan receives a range of interventions to support her academic and transitional needs. Currently, she receives Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) in Study Skills for 258 minutes weekly and participates in college and career awareness programs, each offered for 15 minutes monthly. She is supported in general education classes with accommodations and receives additional support in math skills development. Previous interventions have included SAI through the Resource Specialist Program as a pull-out service for 240 minutes weekly during fourth grade, and short-term counseling from the school psychologist and counselor to review self-regulation strategies and provide transition support during fourth grade.

Current services continue to address her needs in math fluency, written expression, and transition planning, reflecting ongoing efforts to strengthen Emma Rose's academic skills and prepare for post-secondary outcomes.

**IEP / Special Education:**
Emma Rose Callahan has an Individualized Education Program (IEP) in place, with her primary eligibility identified as a Specific Learning Disability (SLD). No mention was found of a 504 plan in her current records. Her IEP addresses academic weaknesses in math fluency, numerical operations, and written expression and includes annual goals aligned with these areas of need, as well as transition supports. Emma Rose was first found eligible for special education services in fourth grade and has continued to receive IEP supports, including specialized academic instruction and accommodations, as she progresses through high school. The IEP team meets regularly to review her progress and adapt programming as needed.

## History of Previous Evaluations

**Previous Evaluations:**
Emma Rose Callahan received an early childhood diagnostic assessment at age three. At the time, her developmental history was notable for exposure to trauma and suspected neglect, with severe neglect reported prior to adoption. Information about her birth was limited, but available details included a birth weight of 6 lb 4 oz and birth in Hollister, CA. Her medical history was remarkable for alleged intrauterine exposure to methamphetamine.

Developmentally, Emma Rose Callahan met most milestones within typical timelines, though she began walking at about 19 months and started speaking around age two, which was later than expected. Early delays in speech, language, and cognitive development were identified, yet she was meeting age-appropriate milestones in both fine and gross motor skills and was toilet trained during the day, despite frequent accidents. 

The assessment included behavioral measures completed by her adoptive mother. Findings from the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) indicated clinically significant withdrawal and somatic complaints. Social development challenges were also noted, as well as concerns in the borderline clinical range for emotional reactivity and oppositional defiance. These early concerns were interpreted with consideration for her complex history, including trauma, neglect, and multiple transitions prior to adoption.

Since coming into the care of her adoptive parents, Emma Rose Callahan has shown developmental progress. Despite early delays and behavioral challenges, at present she maintains age-appropriate communication skills, participates in classroom activities—including physical education—and her handwriting remains legible within expectations for her age.

## Student / Caregiver / Teacher Input

**Parent/Caregiver Input — adoptive mother:**
Emma Rose Callahan’s early history is marked by significant trauma, including severe neglect prior to adoption and suspected exposure to trauma such as abuse and domestic violence. She was reportedly exposed to methamphetamine in utero. Emma Rose was removed from her biological parents’ care at 19 months, spent two weeks in foster care, and then joined her adoptive family, who formally adopted her in June 2013. At age three, her adoptive mother reported that Emma Rose was delayed in both speech/language and overall cognitive development, walking at 19 months and beginning to talk around age two. Emma Rose had no hospitalizations or serious illnesses in early childhood, and medical notes indicate no history of medications or allergies at that time. She was sleeping soundly through the night, napping regularly, and shared a room with her sister. Sensory processing differences were evident, with definite differences compared to her peers’ responses to sensory input (including sensory seeking and sensory sensitivity), and she sometimes required movement breaks to sustain attention. Emma Rose showed social interest, initiated play, and had good attention and cooperation during play-based and structured tasks, though she occasionally needed redirection. Her early development in fine and gross motor and age-appropriate self-care skills was generally on track, though with occasional challenges such as dressing fasteners and overnight dryness. Behaviorally, significant meltdowns and severe aggression were reported, along with clinically significant withdrawal, somatic complaints, emotional reactivity, and difficulties with social development, as reflected in parent rating scales and reports. Her adoptive mother also highlighted clinically significant sensory challenges, safety concerns related to running and escape, and the potential benefit of a weighted blanket for sleep. Emma Rose’s progress in developmental milestones and adaptation to her adoptive family were noted as positives amid these complex early needs.

**Parent/Caregiver Input — classroom teacher:**
Emma Rose Callahan attended Bright Start Preschool, a bilingual Chinese/English program, before entering elementary school. In fourth grade, she attended Oak Meadow School and Creekside Oaks, where her initial IEP was developed. Her teacher highlighted that, aside from walking and talking delays, Emma Rose had generally met developmental milestones. In the classroom, her teacher noted average skills in communication, gross and fine motor, vocational, and adaptive daily living areas. She demonstrated age-appropriate communication and participated in PE with her peers. Her handwriting was usually legible and motor development was not considered an area of concern. The teacher identified specific challenges with attention to instruction, following class rules and directions, and peer interaction—concerns associated with her diagnosis of ADHD. Academically, Emma Rose demonstrated strengths in oral reading fluency, reading comprehension, spelling, essay composition, algebraic concepts, and numerical operations, but was inconsistent with multi-step math word problems and showed below-average performance in math problem-solving and some aspects of math fluency. Formative classroom data showed strengths in reading skills, written composition with some errors, and some areas of math fluency, yet relative weakness in sustained attention during instruction and task follow-through. Her initial plan included pullout support through the Resource Specialist Program (SAI), short-term school counseling for self-regulation, and selected class accommodations to target her academic, executive functioning, and self-regulation goals.

**Student/Client/Patient Input — Student profile and interview:**
Emma Rose Callahan currently attends Ridgeway High School (RIDGEWAY-CORDOVA SELPA) as a ninth grader, having also experienced placement at Options for Youth homeschool in the past. In interview, she described the positive impact of medication on her attention, stating, “Without meds it’s really hard, with meds it’s fine.” She shared a history of recent health interventions, including tonsil removal (resulting in resolution of sleep apnea), and is actively involved in ongoing treatment for sleep disorders such as fitting for a CPAP machine. Emma Rose reports she does not like math but tries to prepare for Math 1 using practice packets, and often works slowly and carefully. She identifies self-confidence as a strength, particularly in writing and public speaking, expressing enjoyment in using metaphors and reflective topics in her essays. She described persistence, stamina, and hard work as personal traits, noting she listens and repeats words until she "gets the words right." Observationally, her reading aloud is described as having a flat tone, but her conversation and reading pace are more typical, with intermittent eye contact. She presents as quiet yet cooperative and is capable of laughing at herself when faced with challenges. During assessment she was generally attentive, though cautious and sometimes impulsive, often self-correcting errors linked to poor attention.

**Parent/Caregiver Input — mom:**
Emma Rose is recognized as a hard-working student who values her grades and cares about her performance. She demonstrates notable strengths in reading, performing at a seventh-grade level per diagnostic data, and has recently scored above grade standard on writing/research tasks, such as essay writing and summarizing health articles for PE. Academic weaknesses remain in the areas of math fluency, numerical operations, math reasoning, and written expression, as reflected in her diagnostic scores and classroom assessments; these areas are the focus of her current IEP goals. Emma Rose receives Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) for Study Skills and Math, general education classes with accommodations, and targeted support in college and career awareness. She is polite, engaged, and helps classmates in Math support; her teachers consistently report she is a pleasure to have in class. Her current plan includes SAI Study Skills (258 minutes/week), specialized instruction, and college/career awareness sessions. Emma Rose exhibits average skills in group work, following instructions, attitude, and peer interactions, but may struggle with motivation at times and is described as shy, particularly in seeking help. She requires medication management for hypothyroidism and takes Geodon, Trileptal, and Vyvanse. There have been health concerns, such as sleep problems (including a CPAP fitting and sleep study), seasonal allergies, and a recent appendectomy, but no current behavioral concerns were reported that would significantly impede her learning.

**Parent/Caregiver Input — mother:**
Emma Rose has a history of ADHD and Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD), with sensitivity to noise and touch also noted. Her mother reflected on recurring sleep issues, complex trauma history associated with adoption, and early delays in speech and walking. Reports indicate ongoing challenges with attention and focus in the classroom environment, which can impact instructional engagement and task completion. Academic needs and goals focus primarily on math fluency, written expression, and necessary supports for successful school transitions.

**Parent/Caregiver Input — Mr. Hollis:**
Mr. Hollis, her physical education and health teacher, notes that Emma Rose is able to locate and summarize health-related articles, demonstrating emerging skills in reading comprehension and written expression within the PE/health context.

**Parent/Caregiver Input — parent:**
The parent perspective from earlier school years described clinically significant behavioral symptoms including aggression, conduct concerns, atypical responses, and challenges with adaptive skills in the home. Ratings from home and school highlighted significant inattention, depression, somatization, and struggles with peer relations and executive functioning. Parents and teachers identified consistent levels of inattention across settings and shared concerns regarding withdrawal, emotional reactivity, and oppositionality, while noting some improvement with supports over time.

**Parent/Caregiver Input — parent/teacher:**
Both parent and teacher ratings converged to indicate clinically significant attention difficulties and concerns regarding depression and somatization. The shared feedback underlined ongoing struggles with peer friendships, executive function, and focus, requiring multi-modal interventions across home and school environments.

**Parent/Caregiver Input — teacher:**
Emma Rose’s teachers, including Mrs. Reed, have noted areas of concern around withdrawal, learning problems, and peer relations, and mild academic or social withdrawal at school. However, hyperactive or disruptive behaviors have not been prominent within the school context, and Emma Rose generally responds well to structured supports and positive teacher relationships.

blocks.prose: Emma Rose Callahan’s early history is marked by significant trauma, including severe neglect prior to adoption and suspected exposure to trauma such as abuse and domestic violence. She was reportedly exposed to methamphetamine in utero. Emma Rose was removed from her biological parents’ care at 19 months, spent two weeks in foster care, and then joined her adoptive family, who formally adopted her in June 2013. At age three, her adoptive mother reported that Emma Rose was delayed in both speech/language and overall cognitive development, walking at 19 months and beginning to talk around age two. Emma Rose had no hospitalizations or serious illnesses in early childhood, and medical notes indicate no history of medications or allergies at that time. She was sleeping soundly through the night, napping regularly, and shared a room with her sister. Sensory processing differences were evident, with definite differences compared to her peers’ responses to sensory input (including sensory seeking and sensory sensitivity), and she sometimes required movement breaks to sustain attention. Emma Rose showed social interest, initiated play, and had good attention and cooperation during play-based and structured tasks, though she occasionally needed redirection. Her early development in fine and gross motor and age-appropriate self-care skills was generally on track, though with occasional challenges such as dressing fasteners and overnight dryness. Behaviorally, significant meltdowns and severe aggression were reported, along with clinically significant withdrawal, somatic complaints, emotional reactivity, and difficulties with social development, as reflected in parent rating scales and reports. Her adoptive mother also highlighted clinically significant sensory challenges, safety concerns related to running and escape, and the potential benefit of a weighted blanket for sleep. Emma Rose’s progress in developmental milestones and adaptation to her adoptive family were noted as positives amid these complex early needs.

Emma Rose Callahan attended Bright Start Preschool, a bilingual Chinese/English program, before entering elementary school. In fourth grade, she attended Oak Meadow School and Creekside Oaks, where her initial IEP was developed. Her teacher highlighted that, aside from walking and talking delays, Emma Rose had generally met developmental milestones. In the classroom, her teacher noted average skills in communication, gross and fine motor, vocational, and adaptive daily living areas. She demonstrated age-appropriate communication and participated in PE with her peers. Her handwriting was usually legible and motor development was not considered an area of concern. The teacher identified specific challenges with attention to instruction, following class rules and directions, and peer interaction—concerns associated with her diagnosis of ADHD. Academically, Emma Rose demonstrated strengths in oral reading fluency, reading comprehension, spelling, essay composition, algebraic concepts, and numerical operations, but was inconsistent with multi-step math word problems and showed below-average performance in math problem-solving and some aspects of math fluency. Formative classroom data showed strengths in reading skills, written composition with some errors, and some areas of math fluency, yet relative weakness in sustained attention during instruction and task follow-through. Her initial plan included pullout support through the Resource Specialist Program (SAI), short-term school counseling for self-regulation, and selected class accommodations to target her academic, executive functioning, and self-regulation goals.

blocks.prose: Emma Rose Callahan currently attends Ridgeway High School (RIDGEWAY-CORDOVA SELPA) as a ninth grader, having also experienced placement at Options for Youth homeschool in the past. In interview, she described the positive impact of medication on her attention, stating, “Without meds it’s really hard, with meds it’s fine.” She shared a history of recent health interventions, including tonsil removal (resulting in resolution of sleep apnea), and is actively involved in ongoing treatment for sleep disorders such as fitting for a CPAP machine. Emma Rose reports she does not like math but tries to prepare for Math 1 using practice packets, and often works slowly and carefully. She identifies self-confidence as a strength, particularly in writing and public speaking, expressing enjoyment in using metaphors and reflective topics in her essays. She described persistence, stamina, and hard work as personal traits, noting she listens and repeats words until she "gets the words right." Observationally, her reading aloud is described as having a flat tone, but her conversation and reading pace are more typical, with intermittent eye contact. She presents as quiet yet cooperative and is capable of laughing at herself when faced with challenges. During assessment she was generally attentive, though cautious and sometimes impulsive, often self-correcting errors linked to poor attention.

Emma Rose is recognized as a hard-working student who values her grades and cares about her performance. She demonstrates notable strengths in reading, performing at a seventh-grade level per diagnostic data, and has recently scored above grade standard on writing/research tasks, such as essay writing and summarizing health articles for PE. Academic weaknesses remain in the areas of math fluency, numerical operations, math reasoning, and written expression, as reflected in her diagnostic scores and classroom assessments; these areas are the focus of her current IEP goals. Emma Rose receives Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) for Study Skills and Math, general education classes with accommodations, and targeted support in college and career awareness. She is polite, engaged, and helps classmates in Math support; her teachers consistently report she is a pleasure to have in class. Her current plan includes SAI Study Skills (258 minutes/week), specialized instruction, and college/career awareness sessions. Emma Rose exhibits average skills in group work, following instructions, attitude, and peer interactions, but may struggle with motivation at times and is described as shy, particularly in seeking help. She requires medication management for hypothyroidism and takes Geodon, Trileptal, and Vyvanse. There have been health concerns, such as sleep problems (including a CPAP fitting and sleep study), seasonal allergies, and a recent appendectomy, but no current behavioral concerns were reported that would significantly impede her learning.

Emma Rose has a history of ADHD and Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD), with sensitivity to noise and touch also noted. Her mother reflected on recurring sleep issues, complex trauma history associated with adoption, and early delays in speech and walking. Reports indicate ongoing challenges with attention and focus in the classroom environment, which can impact instructional engagement and task completion. Academic needs and goals focus primarily on math fluency, written expression, and necessary supports for successful school transitions.

Mr. Hollis, her physical education and health teacher, notes that Emma Rose is able to locate and summarize health-related articles, demonstrating emerging skills in reading comprehension and written expression within the PE/health context.

The parent perspective from earlier school years described clinically significant behavioral symptoms including aggression, conduct concerns, atypical responses, and challenges with adaptive skills in the home. Ratings from home and school highlighted significant inattention, depression, somatization, and struggles with peer relations and executive functioning. Parents and teachers identified consistent levels of inattention across settings and shared concerns regarding withdrawal, emotional reactivity, and oppositionality, while noting some improvement with supports over time.

Both parent and teacher ratings converged to indicate clinically significant attention difficulties and concerns regarding depression and somatization. The shared feedback underlined ongoing struggles with peer friendships, executive function, and focus, requiring multi-modal interventions across home and school environments.

Emma Rose’s teachers, including Mrs. Reed, have noted areas of concern around withdrawal, learning problems, and peer relations, and mild academic or social withdrawal at school. However, hyperactive or disruptive behaviors have not been prominent within the school context, and Emma Rose generally responds well to structured supports and positive teacher relationships.

Sensory processing difficulties were significant, with marked differences noted in how she responded to sensory input compared to peers. Sensory seeking behavior, emotional reactivity, and low endurance/tone were observed. Behaviorally, Emma Rose experienced several meltdowns per week at this age, characterized by screaming and aggression directed at furniture, with difficulty being consoled. Aggressive behavior was mostly limited to these episodes. Standard assessments found clinically significant symptoms in withdrawal, somatic complaints, emotional reactivity, and social development. At age 3, Mrs. Callahan described Emma Rose’s attention as generally good with adult support and the use of positive reinforcement, though redirection was sometimes needed. Emma Rose Callahan participated in an early childhood diagnostic assessment at age three, during which several areas of concern were identified. Developmental history revealed that she met most milestones at expected ages, with exceptions noted for walking, which occurred at 19 months, and developing speech, which began around age two. Delays in speech and language as well as suspected delays in overall cognitive development were documented. At the time of assessment, Emma Rose was meeting age-appropriate milestones in both fine and gross motor skills, was toilet trained during the day (with occasional accidents), and maintained age-appropriate communication skills.

Her birth history was limited, though records indicate a birth weight of 6 pounds 4 ounces and that she was born in Hollister, CA. Medical history is remarkable for alleged in utero exposure to methamphetamine, and her adoption at 19 months followed a period marked by severe neglect. The assessment further noted that Emma’s developmental progress improved after being placed with her adoptive parents.

Concerns related to social-emotional functioning included findings from the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL), which indicated clinically significant withdrawal and somatic complaints. According to her adoptive mother, Emma scored in the borderline clinical range for emotional reactivity and oppositional defiant problems, and in the clinically significant range for somatic complaints, withdrawal, and social development problems.

Overall, the assessment suggested that exposure to neglect and trauma, both prior to and shortly after birth, may have contributed to Emma’s complex developmental needs. The history of trauma and suspected abuse were important contextual factors at the time of the evaluation. Despite these early concerns, Emma showed evidence of ongoing developmental progress and maintained age-appropriate skills in motor and communication domains.

Emma Rose Callahan’s early developmental history is notable for significant adversity, including exposure to trauma and severe neglect prior to adoption. It is reported that she experienced neglect, with trauma suspected, and was removed from her birth parents’ care at 19 months. After two weeks in foster care, she joined her adoptive family and was formally adopted in June 2013. There is a history of alleged in utero exposure to methamphetamine. Her birthweight was reported as 6 lb 4 oz, but other birth details are limited. Early assessments identified delays in speech and language, as well as concerns about global cognitive development. She began walking at 19 months and was using sentences by 3 years old. Emma Rose Callahan attended the Sunshine Bilingual Chinese/English preschool before entering kindergarten. The adoptive mother reported that Emma Rose made developmental progress once in her care, with age-appropriate fine and gross motor development, and increasing independence in self-care activities, such as feeding herself and dressing (except for managing fasteners).

Medical history from this period indicates no significant hospitalizations or surgeries, major illnesses, or allergies, though she is reported to have sensitivity to noise and touch as well as some sleep difficulties (taking 20-30 minutes to fall asleep, sleeping through the night, and napping daily). Emma Rose slept in a pull-up (usually dry in the morning), shared a room with her sister, and sometimes needed a weighted blanket to help settle at night. Sensory processing difficulties were significant, with marked differences noted in how she responded to sensory input compared to peers. Sensory seeking behavior, emotional reactivity, and low endurance/tone were observed. Her mother also reported Emma Rose often needed sensory movement breaks to maintain attention and could have difficulty sustaining focus when her arousal level was low.

Behaviorally, Emma Rose experienced several meltdowns per week at this age, characterized by screaming and aggression directed at furniture, with difficulty being consoled. Aggressive behavior was mostly limited to these episodes. Standard assessments found clinically significant symptoms in withdrawal, somatic complaints, emotional reactivity, and social development. Parent rating scales indicated borderline clinical concerns for oppositional defiance and a range of behaviors associated with ADHD—including inattention and distractibility—were present both at home and school. At age 3, Mrs. Callahan described Emma Rose’s attention as generally good with adult support and the use of positive reinforcement, though redirection was sometimes needed. Safety concerns included running behaviors and escape. Overall, Emma Rose was described as having made notable developmental gains since adoption, but continued to present complex regulatory, sensory, and social-emotional needs.

In fourth grade, Emma Rose was assessed at Fairhaven for her initial Individualized Education Program (IEP) to determine special education eligibility. At that time, her school of residence was Oak Meadow School, and her school of attendance was Creekside Oaks. The teacher reported Emma Rose met most developmental milestones on time, with the exception of walking at 19 months and talking at about 2 years. She began using sentences at about age 3. Emma Rose’s communication skills and participation in PE were not areas of concern, and her handwriting was noted to be legible and within appropriate boundaries for her age.

Academically, the classroom teacher identified Emma Rose as functioning in the below average to average range compared to peers. Strengths were noted in early reading skills, word reading, oral reading fluency, reading comprehension, spelling, essay composition, alphabet writing fluency, and some aspects of numerical operations and math fluency (multiplication), while math problem solving, multi-step word problems, and math fluency (addition/subtraction) were weaker. Writing samples often included errors and sometimes featured run-on or fragmented sentences.

The teacher described attention deficits consistent with a diagnosis of ADHD that impacted Emma Rose's engagement and focus in general education settings. The teacher reported some ongoing concerns in attention to instruction, following classroom standards, peer interaction, and following directions, but indicated that Emma Rose maintained average skills in independence, communication with staff, coping with frustration, and attendance. During classroom or testing experiences, Emma Rose was cooperative and able to complete tasks when presented, though she occasionally required redirection. The IEP prepared at this time provided specialized academic instruction (SAI) via RSP (Resource Specialist Program), as well as short-term counseling with the school psychologist to support self-regulation and transitions. Teacher rating scales and feedback also supported observations of elevated inattention, withdrawal, peer interaction challenges, and behavioral symptoms associated with depression and somatic complaints.

blocks.prose:
Emma Rose Callahan described her current school program as a homeschool arrangement through Options for Youth, where she works on packet-based curriculum, including 'Get Ready for Math 1.' She identified that she works hard and is careful but tends to work slowly. She reported that, without medication, 'it’s really hard, with meds it’s fine,' indicating that medication supports her functioning and concentration. She noted past medical interventions for sleep apnea ('I had my tonsil out and no more sleep apnea') and changes in strategies to improve attention and alertness at school.

Emma Rose expressed a positive sense of self-confidence in some areas and stated she does not enjoy math but showed pride in her effort and stamina. She enjoys creative expression in writing, stating, 'In my writing I like to use metaphors like a river or an animal. I wrote an essay about life and what happens when we die,' and expressed an interest in public speaking. She described her strategy for learning new words as listening repeatedly until accuracy is achieved. When reading aloud, her tone is described as flat; however, her pace is natural for both oral reading and conversations. During the interview and assessment, she was cooperative, persistent, sometimes complained when tasks were hard but was able to laugh at herself. Eye contact during conversation was quiet and intermittent. In terms of attention and concentration, she described herself as cautious but sometimes impulsive; she often self-corrected and acknowledged occasional errors due to poor attention.

At her current high school, Ridgeway High, Emma Rose Callahan is enrolled under RIDGEWAY-CORDOVA SELPA, with her IEP specifying a primary eligibility of Specific Learning Disability (SLD). She receives Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) in both Math and Study Skills (258 minutes weekly), as well as college and career awareness services. Recent IEP documentation notes that she entered FHS (Fairhaven) with SAI English and Study Skills, and now attends Ridgeway High following a period of enrollment in private school by her parents.

Emma Rose demonstrates persistent academic weakness in math fluency/numerical operations, written language, and transition skills. Current areas of instructional need are specifically identified as math fluency, written expression, and postsecondary transition. She is also reported to have difficulties in attention, focus, and self-motivation, though she is able to follow directions and shows average skills in group work, independence, peer interactions, and attitude toward learning. Teachers and her mother note that Emma Rose is shy, which limits her ability to seek help. There are, however, no behaviors of concern that impede her learning in the classroom.

Emma Rose has had some health concerns, including hypothyroidism (medicated, currently titrating dosage), is prescribed Geodon, Trileptal, and Vyvanse, and is being fitted for a CPAP device for ongoing sleep problems. At the beginning of the year, she regularly fell asleep in morning classes but now uses strategies such as taking breaks and drinking water to remain alert. Her overall attendance is good, and she is described as caring about her grades and giving her best effort. She is currently reading at the 7th grade level (per Edmentum diagnostic), and in math, her scores indicate specific difficulties with algebra, fractions, ratios, geometry, measurement, and operations. She has struggled on vocabulary assessments (15/25 on a recent quiz) and has a diagnostic math score at the 18th percentile. Despite these areas of difficulty, her writing is sometimes described as 'above standard,' and she recently scored an 86% on a summative assessment.

The IEP outlines math and writing goals, such as solving five multi-step linear equations and writing two-paragraph essays with grade-appropriate conventions and organization. Emma Rose takes her classwork seriously, assists other students, and has been described as polite and engaged in her support class. Written feedback describes her as a pleasure to teach and a student who “puts in a lot of work" and "cares about her grades."

Emma Rose’s mother adds that her daughter has a history of ADHD and has displayed sensory sensitivity to noise and touch since early childhood. Emma Rose experienced sleep problems which have persisted but are being addressed via medical and behavioral interventions. She has also been diagnosed with Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD) in addition to ADHD. The mother reports sensitivity to sensory input that remains different from peer responses. 

Throughout her history, Emma Rose has experienced clinically significant symptoms in several behavioral and social-emotional domains, including depression, withdrawal, somatic complaints, and executive functioning difficulties. These concerns are sometimes more prominent at home, where clinically significant levels of inattention, defiance/aggression, and struggles in peer relations have been observed. She has also experienced meltdowns and aggressive behaviors most commonly in the home setting, but these have not been reported as impacting her current classroom learning.

Mr. Hollis reports that Emma Rose is capable of engaging with academic tasks that connect content to real-world topics. For example, in health and physical education, she has been successful in finding articles related to class topics and writing summaries about them. This skill reflects her capacity for research and written expression in structured settings, supporting the observation that writing—while an area of need—can also be a strength when she is provided with clear parameters and support.

Parent rating scales and interviews confirm that Emma Rose has exhibited clinically significant behavioral symptoms associated with aggression, conduct problems, atypical behaviors, and adaptive skills deficits in home and school environments. Parents have observed very elevated symptoms of depression, somatization, and executive functioning problems, with notable concerns in peer relationships and home behavior regulation. Both home and school reports have highlighted high levels of inattention related to ADHD, as well as periods of withdrawal and difficulty with adaptive functioning.

Both parent and teacher rating scales indicate clinically significant inattention and attention problems in both settings, along with shared concerns related to depression and somatization. Attention variability has been observed, with Emma Rose benefitting from sensory breaks and adult prompts. Concerns about social engagement and peer relations are also noted as ongoing challenges.

Mrs. Reed, a past classroom teacher, identified concerns in the areas of peer relations, withdrawal, learning challenges, and attention in fourth grade. She reported significant learning problems and social withdrawal at school. However, hyperactive behaviors were not a concern in the classroom during her observation period. Teacher feedback has consistently highlighted Emma Rose’s learning difficulties and challenges relating to peers, while also confirming that disruptive or externalizing behaviors are not observed at school.

Emma Rose Callahan was adopted at 19 months, and information about her birth family is limited. Her adoptive mother reports a family history of ADHD. At 19 months of age, she entered her current family through adoption. In elementary school, Emma attended Creekside Oaks and later was designated as a resident student at Oak Meadow School. By fourth grade, assessment data indicated that she was functioning academically within the below average to average range compared to same-age peers, with strengths in oral reading fluency, reading comprehension, spelling, essay composition, alphabet writing fluency, and numerical operations. She could read grade level text at 52 correct words per minute and answer comprehension questions with 71% accuracy. She was also able to add within 100 with 93% accuracy, subtract within 100 with 83% accuracy, and multiply within 100 with 88% accuracy. Word problem-solving and written expression with conventions, however, were areas of inconsistent performance.

Emma transitioned to Ridgeway High School and is enrolled in the Ridgeway-Cordova SELPA, currently in ninth grade. Her attendance is noted to be good, and she is able to follow directions in class. She has a diagnostic score of 989, ranking at the 18th national percentile, and is working at a seventh grade reading level, according to Edmentum diagnostic data. On recent assessments, she demonstrated above standard performance in writing/research, scored 86% on her latest summative assessment, and continues to work actively on improving her math fluency, numerical operations, and written expression. In math, Emma scored 3 out of 11 on Algebra & Expressions, 3 out of 11 on Fractions & Ratios, 3 out of 10 on Geometry, 1 out of 11 on Measurement, Data & Statistics, and 5 out of 11 on Numbers & Operations, highlighting continuing needs in these areas. Literature and informational text scores were 8 out of 15 each, while vocabulary was 5 out of 14, and she recently earned 15 out of 25 on a vocabulary quiz. Math fluency, written expression, and transition continue to be documented areas of need for goals in her current IEP.

Records and student interview also indicate Emma was previously enrolled in a private school through parental placement and participated in Options for Youth home school. She has worked on math preparation and essay-writing, showing personal interest in using metaphors and creative writing. Emma describes herself as someone who listens repeatedly until accuracy is achieved and feels she would be good at public speaking, despite not enjoying math. Emma Rose Callahan’s adoptive mother provided extensive background information reflecting a history of trauma prior to adoption, including suspected severe neglect and alleged intrauterine exposure to methamphetamine. Emma Rose was removed from her biological parents' care to a foster home for two weeks before being placed with her adoptive family at 19 months and formally adopted shortly thereafter. Significant delays in speech, language, and overall cognitive development were reported at age three, as well as late walking (at 19 months). Medical records from early childhood indicate no hospitalizations, surgeries, or significant illnesses or injuries at that time. Emma Rose attended a bilingual preschool and demonstrated the ability to separate easily from her adoptive mother, showing good social interest, eye contact, and engagement in play. Early assessments described her speech as sometimes unclear but generally effective for communication.

The family reported Emma Rose was meeting milestones in fine and gross motor skills and self-care except for challenges managing clothing fasteners. She required daytime reminders for toileting and slept well, sharing a room with her sister. Sensory processing difficulties were noted, with significant sensory seeking, emotional reactivity, and differences from peers in response to sensory input. Emma Rose benefitted from movement breaks to sustain attention but had issues with inattention, distractibility, and occasional safety concerns related to running/escape behaviors. Meltdowns, featuring severe aggression (screaming, hitting furniture), occurred 2–5 times per week.

Parental, teacher, and standardized behavior ratings from this period indicated clinically significant problems in withdrawal, somatic complaints, depression, emotional reactivity, and oppositional and aggressive behaviors. Caregivers also endorsed significant inattention and noted struggles with peer relations, defiance, executive functioning, and adaptive skills. Over time, Emma Rose demonstrated developmental progress in the adoptive home, but the early history of neglect has been considered a contributing factor in her ongoing emotional and behavioral needs.

In fourth grade at Oak Meadow School (residence school) and Creekside Oaks (school of attendance), Emma Rose Callahan was identified for an initial Individualized Education Program (IEP) to determine eligibility for special education. The classroom teacher noted that Emma Rose met all developmental milestones except for delayed walking and talking. She displayed age-appropriate communication, handwriting, and gross/fine motor abilities, with self-care skills comparable to her peers. She attended PE with her class and required no accommodations in motor or communication realms. However, chronic difficulties were observed in attention to instruction, compliance with class standards, peer interactions, and following directions—challenges attributed to her diagnosis of ADHD.

Academically, Emma Rose functioned in the below average to average range compared to peers, with relative strengths in early reading, reading comprehension, oral reading fluency, spelling, essay composition, alphabet writing fluency, and some numerical operations. She presented weaknesses in math problem solving, math fluency (addition and subtraction), and multi-step word problems. Benchmarks showed she could perform single-step operations with high accuracy but inconsistently solved multi-step tasks. Written expression revealed strengths in generating ideas but ongoing challenges with mechanics and organization. Standardized assessments and observations highlighted average cognitive abilities in crystallized and long-term retrieval skills, with weaknesses noted in fluid reasoning and short-term memory. Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) and short-term school counseling were provided. Behavioral observations at school showed no significant hyperactivity but did note inattention, withdrawal, learning problems, and difficulty with peer relations.

blocks.prose:
Emma Rose Callahan communicated that medication plays a significant role in her ability to function: "Without meds it’s really hard, with meds it’s fine." She reported history of medical intervention, including a tonsillectomy that resolved sleep apnea. During the interview, Emma Rose described receiving her education through Options for Youth home school, currently working through packets to prepare for Math 1. She described a dislike of math, noting it as an area of reduced self-confidence, but expressed willingness to work hard and reported good stamina, though she works slowly and carefully.

Emma Rose is proud of her progress in writing and enjoys using metaphors and exploring philosophical topics such as life and death in essays. She listens and practices repeatedly until she masters the language and expressed interest in public speaking. In testing and conversation, she demonstrated a flat tone when reading aloud, normal conversation pace, intermittent eye contact, and was generally cooperative—persisting through challenges, sometimes complaining but able to laugh at herself. She described herself as cautious and sometimes impulsive, often self-correcting but also making occasional errors due to inattention.

In ninth grade at Ridgeway High School (RIDGEWAY-CORDOVA SELPA), Emma Rose Callahan is supported through an IEP for a primary diagnosis of Specific Learning Disability, with longstanding ADHD and Reactive Attachment Disorder. She receives services including Specialized Academic Instruction, Study Skills, college and career awareness, and accommodations within the general education classroom. The IEP team and her mother identified academic weaknesses in math fluency, numerical operations, math reasoning, and written expression as areas of ongoing need.

Emma Rose’s math assessment results reflected below average performance in Algebra, Fractions, Geometry, Measurement/Data/Statistics, and basic number operations, with an overall diagnostic rank at the 18th national percentile. Her strengths included more basic computation skills and ability to solve simple linear equations once given support and practice. Written work was characterized as above standard in some measures but consistently reflected challenges in organization, grammar, and mechanics; recent goals have focused on structured two-paragraph expository writing. Reading diagnostics placed Emma Rose at a 7th grade level, with moderate performance on vocabulary and comprehension tasks.

Mom noted that Emma Rose is generally shy, which may limit her willingness to request help. At school, she has good attendance and follows directions, and her behaviors do not impede learning, though attention and motivation have been described as variable. Emma Rose is receiving medication management for hypothyroid and ADHD (including Vyvance, Geodon, and Trileptal). Past health issues include an appendectomy and pending sleep study for ongoing sleep problems. Supports target not only academics but also self-regulation, social-emotional adjustment, and post-secondary transition.

Emma Rose Callahan’s mother reiterated a complex history, highlighting ongoing ADHD, sensitivity to noise and touch, and a background of trauma and adoption. She described recurring concerns around sleep and seasonal allergies. In elementary school, sleep issues sometimes prompted recommendations for weighted blankets or movement breaks to enhance regulation and attention. Sensory processing difficulties continue to impact Emma Rose’s comfort in various environments.

Mr. Hollis, Emma Rose Callahan’s physical education teacher, reported that Emma Rose is capable of completing academic tasks aligned to course content, including reading an article related to health or PE and producing a summary. He noted that she participates appropriately in assignments and demonstrates the ability to meet expectations when provided structure and support.

Parental rating scales and interviews indicated clinically significant behaviors related to aggression, conduct problems, atypicality, and depressed mood. Concerns included pronounced difficulties in executive functioning, peer relations, and adaptive skills at home. Shared concerns with educators focused on somatization, depression, and attention difficulties. These patterns have been consistent from early childhood through the school years, with clinical ratings indicating elevated symptoms in both home and school contexts.

Both parent and teacher observations supported the presence of significant inattention (attributable to ADHD), emotional difficulties, and academic struggles. Concerns related to depression, somatic complaints, and attention problems were corroborated in multiple settings. Notably, clinically significant inattention has been observed in both school and home environments, influencing Emma Rose Callahan’s learning, engagement, and at times, peer interactions.

Emma Rose Callahan’s fourth grade teacher, Mrs. Reed, documented additional school-based concerns in the domains of withdrawal, learning problems, and positive peer relations. She highlighted the absence of significant hyperactivity at school in contrast with reported home behaviors. Mrs. Reed’s academic observations aligned with standardized assessment results, noting academic strengths in reading, oral reading fluency, and specific aspects of writing, but persistent areas of difficulty in attention, multi-step math reasoning, writing mechanics, and class participation. Mrs. Reed’s input underscores the ongoing interplay of academic, social, and attention-related factors in Emma Rose’s educational journey.

Emma Rose was removed from her biological parents’ care at 19 months due to severe neglect and suspected trauma, and placed with her adoptive family, where she was formally adopted at age 3. There is a history of alleged intrauterine exposure to methamphetamine. Information about her birth is limited, except that she was born in Hollister, CA, with a birth weight of 6 lb 4 oz. Before adoption, Emma Rose experienced significant neglect, which, along with possible trauma, is believed to have contributed to her early delays.

Developmentally, Emma Rose walked at about 19 months and began talking around 2 years, using early sentences by age 3. Her adoptive mother noted delays in speech, language, and overall cognitive development as a young child. She attended Bright Start Preschool, a bilingual Chinese/English program. Emma Rose did not experience hospitalizations, surgeries, or major illnesses aside from normal childhood events, and had no allergies or chronic health conditions at that stage. Her sleep patterns were generally healthy: she slept well at night, napped daily, and shared a room with her sister.

Emma Rose was described as having progressed developmentally since being in her adoptive family. At age 3, she could dress herself except for managing fasteners like buttons, and could unzip zippers. She was able to feed herself using utensils or her fingers and was toilet trained during the day but continued to have frequent accidents. Her mother noted that Emma Rose might benefit from strategies such as weighted blankets for sleep and sensory movement breaks for attention. Sensory processing difficulties, sensory seeking, emotional reactivity, and inattention/distractibility were observed. Meltdowns occurred two to five times per week, during which Emma Rose might scream, hit furniture, and be difficult to console; these episodes sometimes included aggression.

Behavioral ratings completed during early childhood reflected significant withdrawal, aggression, oppositional defiant tendencies, emotional reactivity, and somatic complaints at a clinically significant level. Social development problems and adaptive skill concerns were also endorsed. Her mother emphasized definite differences in sensory processing compared to peers and noted specific challenges with attention, arousal levels, and executive functioning. Despite these early challenges, Emma Rose displayed social interest, good eye contact, and positive responsiveness to praise and reinforcement.

In fourth grade, Emma Rose Callahan was attending Oak Meadow School as her residence school and participated in PE and classroom activities with her same-age peers. At the time of her initial Fairhaven IEP, she was receiving some Specialized Academic Instruction and resource support due to attentional challenges and academic needs, particularly in math and written language. The classroom teacher described Emma Rose as maintaining age-appropriate communication, motor, and self-care skills, and noted her handwriting as typically legible and appropriate. Independence in self-care, interaction with staff, coping with frustration, and attendance/punctuality were all reported to be at an average level for her age.

Areas of concern for the classroom teacher included attention to instruction, following directions and class standards, and social interactions with peers. Behaviors such as withdrawal, peer struggles, and learning problems were identified, although significant hyperactivity was not observed in the school setting. Emma Rose was described as cooperative in testing situations, able to complete tasks, but demonstrating below average to average academic functioning compared to peers. Math fluency (especially with addition and subtraction) and problem solving were identified as weaker areas, while oral reading fluency, reading comprehension, spelling, essay composition, and numerical operations were highlighted as areas of relative strength. Math fluency and written expression remained target areas for growth through her elementary years.

Accommodations and short-term school counseling were initiated to support self-regulation and adjustment.

blocks.prose:
Emma Rose Callahan provided her perspective on her learning strengths and challenges. She reported that medication is effective in supporting her attention and functioning: “Without meds it’s really hard, with meds it’s fine.” Emma Rose noted a history of sleep problems, including previously having sleep apnea, for which she underwent a tonsillectomy with resolution. She is currently homeschooled through the Options for Youth program, and describes working through math packets as preparation for Math 1.

Emma Rose describes herself as a hardworking student with good stamina, who works slowly and carefully. She readily acknowledges that math is not her favorite subject, while expressing greater self-confidence and interest in writing. She enjoys using metaphors in her composition and has written reflective essays on broad concepts, such as life and what happens after death. She is interested in public speaking and practices her writing and oral work until she “gets the words right.”

Emma Rose describes her own reading as fluent in terms of pace during both conversation and silent reading, though her tone may be flat when reading aloud. She presents as quiet in conversation, with intermittent eye contact. During testing and interview, she was described as cooperative, persistent, at times complaining when tasks were difficult but able to laugh at herself. Her attention and concentration are generally cautious, though she may sometimes be impulsive and self-correct errors as they arise.

Emma Rose is currently in ninth grade at Ridgeway High School, after attending several schools including Oak Meadow, Creekside Oaks, and Bright Start Preschool. She participates in the Ridgeway-Cordova SELPA and has an Individualized Education Program (IEP) in place for a primary eligibility of Specific Learning Disability (SLD). Recent academic reporting from mom and teachers confirms ongoing weaknesses in math fluency, numerical operations, and written language. Emma Rose receives specialized academic instruction and support in study skills, as well as general education accommodations. She also participates in college and career awareness programs monthly.

Mom reported that Emma Rose was diagnosed with hypothyroidism and takes daily medications (Geodon, Trileptal, and Vyvanse). She has a history of RAD, ADHD, and sleep problems. Emma Rose is currently being fitted for a CPAP machine and will participate in a sleep study over the summer. At the beginning of the year, Emma Rose struggled with daytime sleepiness, especially in morning classes, although she now proactively seeks breaks when needed. There are no current significant medical or allergy concerns impacting her schooling. She is reading at approximately a 7th grade level, according to the Edmentum diagnostic assessment, with specific needs in vocabulary and language.

Emma Rose’s most significant areas of need include math fluency, math computation and reasoning, written expression, and transition skills. She has goals related to solving linear equations and writing multi-paragraph essays with supporting details and appropriate conventions, which have shown progress over the past year. Her teachers describe her as polite, engaged, hardworking, and helpful with peers. She is generally able to follow directions and does not have behaviors that impede her learning, though she continues to experience shyness, which impacts her advocacy for help in class or with assignments.

Emma Rose’s mother consistently reports a history of ADHD, emotional and sensory challenges, and difficulties with self-regulation, attention, and transitions. Sensitivity to noise and touch is noted, as well as continuing sleep issues and seasonal allergies. These historical and ongoing needs have influenced Emma Rose’s academic functioning, especially in the context of her early trauma and developmental delays. The family remains involved in coordinating medical care and supports in conjunction with her IEP team.

Mr. Hollis, Emma Rose’s health and physical education teacher, observed that she is capable of independently finding a health-related article and composing a summary. This reflects her growing skills in research and written expression when the assignment is meaningful and structured.

Parental behavior ratings completed previously have described clinically significant concerns regarding aggression, conduct problems, atypicality, adaptive skills, executive functioning (home), and peer relations. Depression, attention/somatic concerns, and defiant/aggressive behaviors have all been prominent at various times. Most recently, the home environment does not show behaviors that impede Emma Rose’s learning at school, but inattention and slow processing persist. Peer interactions have improved overall, though some challenges are still present, especially in new or unstructured settings.

Parent and teacher rating scales both show high scores for inattention and shared concerns around depression, somatization, and attention problems. In classroom settings, Emma Rose continues to benefit from consistent supports, clear expectations, and frequent check-ins to sustain engagement and address emerging needs.

In teacher ratings, Mrs. Reed highlighted additional concerns in the areas of withdrawal, peer relations, and learning difficulties. She did not observe significant levels of hyperactivity within the classroom, but emphasized the need for targeted support in attention, compliance with classroom routines, and the strengthening of peer connections through positive social experiences.

Emma Rose has diagnoses of Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD) and ADHD. Emma Rose Callahan's early developmental history is notable for exposure to significant prenatal and early childhood trauma. According to her adoptive mother, Emma was reportedly exposed to methamphetamines in utero. She was removed from her biological parents due to severe neglect, spending two weeks in foster care before joining her adoptive family at 19 months; Emma was formally adopted in June 2013. Hospitalizations, surgeries, other significant illnesses, or allergies were not reported during early childhood, and there was no regular medication use at that time. Emma’s initial delays included walking at 19 months and speech/language delays, with suspected global cognitive delays. There was no information on her birth beyond her birthweight (6 lbs 4 oz) and location (Hollister, CA).

Emma attended a bilingual Chinese/English preschool, demonstrating gradual developmental progress once in the care of her adoptive family. She separated easily from her mother for evaluation, showed social interest and appropriate eye contact, and used simple sentences, though her speech was sometimes unclear. The adoptive mother noted improvements in social interaction, turn taking, and the emergence of age-appropriate self-care, fine, and gross motor skills, with persistent difficulty during emotional outbursts. Meltdowns, typically 2-5 times per week, involved screaming, hitting furniture, and difficulty consoling. These episodes often included severe aggression. There were clinically significant findings for withdrawal, somatic complaints, emotional reactivity, and oppositional behaviors based on parent report and rating scales. Sensory processing difficulties were also reported, including heightened sensitivity to sensory input and differences in how Emma responded compared to same-age peers. Emma sometimes benefited from sensory movement breaks to maintain attention. Within daily routines, she was able to dress herself (except for fasteners), unzip zippers, feed herself with utensils or by hand, and was day toilet trained but had frequent accidents. Emma generally slept well, although she needed 20–30 minutes to fall asleep and sometimes benefited from a weighted blanket. Safety concerns around running/escape behaviors were also described.

Emma’s early care and family stability correlated with steady developmental progress, though profiles of emotional reactivity, sensory need, and attention difficulties persisted as areas of concern.

Emma’s fourth-grade classroom teacher described her as academically functioning within the below average to average range compared to same-age peers. Her strengths included early reading skills, oral reading fluency, reading comprehension, spelling, essay composition, alphabet writing fluency, and certain numerical operations. Scores for math fluency in multiplication were comparatively strong, while math fluency in addition and subtraction, as well as math problem solving and multi-step problems, were areas of need. The teacher noted that Emma maintained age-appropriate communication, motor, vocational, and adaptive living skills, and her handwriting was legible and appropriately formed. The most pressing areas of difficulty were attention to instruction, following class standards, peer interaction, and following directions.

Emma’s academic profile was further characterized by average performance in crystallized intelligence, long-term storage and retrieval, visual and auditory processing, and processing speed, but with relative weaknesses in fluid reasoning and short-term memory. Her work habits and independence in self-care, interaction with staff, coping with frustration, and attendance/punctuality were noted as average. During testing, Emma was cooperative and able to complete all subtests presented. Interventions provided at Fairhaven included SAI (Resource Specialist) pull-out services for 240 minutes per week, as well as targeted short-term counseling to address self-regulation and transition skills. The teacher reported that Emma was reading at a seventh-grade level by diagnostic assessment, and that she could read grade-level text at 52–85 correct words per minute, answering comprehension questions with 70–75% accuracy. Writing samples indicated strengths in organizing ideas and text structure, but included errors in conventions such as subject/verb agreement, punctuation, and spelling. Math performance showed proficiency with basic operations but inconsistency with multi-step problems. In the classroom, she also exhibited some difficulties with motivation and attention/focus.

blocks.prose:
Emma Rose Callahan described her experience in school and at home from her perspective during interview and direct assessment. Regarding attention and focus, she reported that being off medication made it 'really hard,' but with medication, tasks were manageable. She shared that, after having her tonsils removed, her sleep apnea improved, and she was being evaluated for a CPAP machine. Emma currently participates in a home school program through Options for Youth, especially for math packet work in preparation for Math 1.

Emma expressed a preference for reading and writing, explaining that she enjoys using metaphors and has written essays on broad topics such as life and what happens after death. She reported that she listens to materials repeatedly until she knows the words, and she feels she would be good at public speaking. However, math is not a favorite subject. Emma described herself as hardworking with good stamina, though she tends to work slowly and carefully. In reading aloud, she demonstrates a flat tone but maintains a normal pace, and in conversation she is generally quiet with intermittent eye contact.

She was noted as cooperative in formal assessments, persistent even when challenged by difficult tasks, and able to self-correct when errors were made due to inattention or impulsivity. Emma sometimes complained about difficult assignments but maintained a sense of humor and was able to laugh at herself. She acknowledged that self-confidence was a relative strength but also said she does not like math.

Emma Rose Callahan is currently in ninth grade at Ridgeway High School and remains on an Individualized Education Program (IEP), with eligibility as a student with a Specific Learning Disability (SLD). She currently receives Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) and Study Skills support, as well as college and career awareness services. Math fluency/numerical operations, written language, and transition skills are identified IEP goal areas. She is reading at a seventh-grade level based on diagnostic evaluation, but she continues to demonstrate weakness in foundational math and writing skills. Emma's diagnostic score in math computation (989) currently places her at the 18th national percentile, consistent with ongoing needs in math fluency and multi-step numerical reasoning. Most recent classroom assessments showed considerable growth, with an 86% score on her last summative assessment.

Emma’s mother reports that she is shy, which can make it difficult for her to advocate for herself or ask for help. Nonetheless, Emma is described as having good attendance, following directions well, and not having any behaviors that impede her learning. At the start of the school year, Emma was observed to fall asleep in morning classes, which her mother connects to sleep problems. She reports a diagnosis of hypothyroidism (with medication adjustments ongoing), ADHD, and Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD). Emma recently underwent medical procedures for sleep concerns, including upcoming sleep studies and CPAP evaluation. She is also prescribed Geodon, Trileptal, and Vyvance, and takes medication for hypothyroidism and seasonal allergies. No health plan is needed at this time, but her mother is in communication with the school regarding changes.

Emma participates in general education with accommodations and receives SAI support in math, alongside services for study skills, college, and career awareness. Her mother notes that Emma takes her classwork seriously, helps peers, and is polite and engaged in her Math support class. Overall, she cares about her grades, shows steady effort, and has shown progress in both written expression and multi-step equation solving when provided structure and support.

Emma’s mother described longstanding attention, behavioral, and sensory concerns. She reports a history of ADHD and noted symptoms such as sensitivity to noise/touch, periods of withdrawal, and variable attention. Past seasons have included sleep problems and episodes of emotional reactivity. Historically, Emma presented with meltdowns, aggression (especially during meltdowns), and episodes of difficulty managing frustration, which were more prominent in earlier years. By fourth grade, rating scales indicated clinically significant and borderline scores in the areas of attention, aggression, withdrawal, somatic concerns, emotional reactivity, and oppositional/defiant behavior. Clinically significant symptoms associated with adaptive skills, depression, executive functioning, and peer relationships were reported through parent rating scales.

Her mother added that Emma demonstrated significant differences in sensory processing, including seeking sensory input and reacting differently than peers to sounds, touch, and other sensations. Emma benefits from movement breaks to help maintain attention. Safety issues have also arisen during running/escape behaviors. While Emma has progressed and matured in many areas, challenges with motivation, focus, and peer relationships continue to require ongoing support.

Mr. Hollis, Emma’s Health and Physical Education teacher, reports that Emma Rose Callahan is able to find health-related articles and write effective summaries about them. This demonstrates her ability to engage with informational text and practice written language skills within a content area, and supports observations of writing strengths and progress on classroom goals.

Additional parent input has highlighted clinically significant behavioral symptoms within the home, particularly related to aggression, conduct problems, atypical behaviors, adaptive skills, depression, executive functioning, defiance, and difficulties with peer relations. These concerns were echoed in teacher and parent rating scales, indicating the need for continued support in emotional and behavioral regulation both at school and home. Shared concerns with the education team include inattention, emotional concerns such as depression and somatization, and challenges with maintaining consistent attention and motivation.

Both parent and teacher reporters have observed clinically significant levels of inattention in school and home settings. Concerns are also shared regarding depression, somatization, and persistent attention problems. While Emma's inattention and focus present challenges across settings, hyperactivity has not been observed as a significant behavior in the school environment.

Teachers in the elementary and current settings have noted additional concerns regarding social withdrawal, learning challenges, and peer interactions. Mrs. Reed, a previous teacher, reported specific concerns about Emma’s learning difficulties, elevated concern around her ability to engage in positive peer relationships, and withdrawal in the classroom. However, significant hyperactive behaviors were not observed at school. Overall, Emma has responded to school-based supports and interventions and remains polite, cooperative, and engaged with support in place.

Emma Rose Callahan’s early developmental history is notable for complex needs related to trauma and neglect prior to her adoption. According to her adoptive mother, Emma Rose experienced severe neglect and was removed from her biological parents’ care at 19 months, living briefly in foster care before joining her adoptive family, with the adoption finalized at age three. There is suspected history of in utero exposure to methamphetamines. Early records note delays in speech and language and overall cognitive development, with walking achieved at 19 months and verbal sentences emerging around age three. She attended a bilingual Chinese/English preschool (Sunshine/Bright Start) and has since demonstrated progress developmentally within her adoptive family’s care.

Medically, Emma Rose has not had hospitalizations or surgeries during early childhood, and no allergies or chronic medical conditions were noted at that time. Sleep has historically been adequate with no snoring or nightmares, though a weighted blanket was recommended for self-regulation at bedtime.

Behaviorally, the adoptive mother reported frequent meltdowns (2–5 times per week), characterized by screaming, hitting furniture, and difficulty consoling, along with episodes of severe aggression. Parent reports and previous behavioral checklists indicated clinically significant symptoms of withdrawal, somatic complaints, emotional reactivity, and oppositional behavior; these concerns were believed to connect to her trauma history. Sensory processing difficulties, including significant differences in sensory responses compared to peers, were observed. Emma Rose benefited from sensory movement breaks and showed issues with sustaining attention, especially when her arousal was low. Nonetheless, she achieved developmental milestones in fine and gross motor skills and was able to perform age-appropriate self-care, with minimal support needed for fasteners while dressing. Safety concerns were noted related to running and elopement behaviors.

Emma Rose Callahan’s fourth-grade classroom teacher at Oak Meadow School (residence school) and Creekside Oaks (school of attendance per IEP) described her as functioning academically between the below average and average range in comparison to peers. She demonstrated age appropriate communication skills and maintained legible, appropriately bounded handwriting. While her gross and fine motor skills and adaptive daily living abilities were not areas of concern, she exhibited some difficulty in attention to instruction, following class standards, following directions, and peer interaction. The teacher also noted strengths in independence with self-care, interacting with staff, and coping with frustration.

Academic assessment indicated relative strengths in early reading skills, oral reading fluency, reading comprehension, spelling, essay composition, alphabet writing fluency, and numerical operations. Weaknesses were more apparent in reading and math problem solving and in math fluency (addition and subtraction). Emma Rose’s performance in crystallized intelligence, long-term storage and retrieval, visual and auditory processing, and processing speed was average, with personal weaknesses in areas of fluid reasoning and short-term memory. Teacher and parent/teacher reflections commented on concerns with attention deficits (associated with ADHD) that were impacting her engagement and focus in class. During testing, she was cooperative and able to complete each subtest as presented.
