blocks.prose:
Emma Rose describes herself as hardworking, detail-oriented, and persistent, though she works slowly and carefully. She shared that medication helps her manage daily tasks, reporting, “Without meds it’s really hard, with meds it’s fine.” She indicated that her sleep apnea improved following a tonsillectomy, and she is currently enrolled in Options for Youth homeschool. In academics, Emma Rose reported that she is preparing for Math 1 through packet-based work, but acknowledges that math is an area of struggle and not her favorite subject. She enjoys writing and expressed a preference for including metaphor in her assignments, highlighting an essay she wrote about life and what happens when we die. Emma Rose demonstrated insight into effective strategies for learning, sharing, "I listen over and over till I get the words right," and expressed interest in public speaking.

The testing interaction noted that Emma Rose presented with a flat tone when reading aloud, though her pace normalized when speaking conversationally. Her eye contact was quiet and intermittent. In assessments, she was cooperative, persistent, and able to self-correct, often laughing at personal errors. She displayed some impulsivity but frequently attempted to self-correct and refocus, although occasional errors arose from lapses in attention. Overall, she described herself as self-confident, with challenges primarily in mathematics.

Emma Rose is currently a ninth grade student enrolled at Ridgeway High School, with all meetings held virtually and supported by the Ridgeway-Cordova SELPA. She has an Individualized Education Program (IEP) in place with a primary eligibility of Specific Learning Disability (SLD), and the IEP team recently determined she would pursue an Alternative Pathway to a Diploma. Her mother reports that Emma Rose came into high school with Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) in English and Study Skills, and continues to receive SAI support, college awareness, and career awareness as part of her programming. The current IEP does not note behaviors that impede her learning nor the need for a 504 plan; behaviors such as shyness are noted as impacting Emma Rose’s ability to ask for help in class. No behaviors have been observed that impede the learning of herself or others.

Regarding her academics, Emma Rose demonstrates notable weaknesses in math fluency/numerical operations, written language, and transition skills, which are reflected as areas of need on her IEP goals. Her most recent diagnostic assessment placed her in the 18th national percentile overall, with specific challenges in Algebra & Expressions, Fractions & Ratios, Geometry, and Measurement, Data, and Statistics. Her mother further reports that she struggles with motivation in classes and has a history of sleep issues that have included daytime sleepiness in class; she is currently undergoing a sleep study and CPAP fitting and has successfully addressed obstructive sleep apnea with a prior tonsillectomy.

Emma Rose is also diagnosed with hypothyroid and takes several medications (Geodon, Trileptal, Vyvance), along with support for seasonal allergies. She uses Study Skills support, has satisfactory attendance, and is able to follow directions. Her mother notes she is reading at a seventh-grade level (per recent diagnostic testing) and has shown progress in writing (scoring 75% accuracy on recent expository essays). Emma Rose cares about her grades, gives strong effort, and is described by staff as polite, engaged, and a pleasure to have in class.

Emma Rose’s mother reports a longstanding history of ADHD and Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD), as well as sensitivities to noise and touch. There is a history of sleep problems, including benefit from routines and intervention for sleep apnea, and intermittent daytime fatigue. Emma Rose continues to need supports for sensory processing difference and regulation. She was adopted at 19 months, with limited available information about her biological family or birth history. Most developmental milestones were achieved in the typical range, though walking and language were both delayed slightly.

Emma Rose receives medications and is closely followed for her health needs. There is no current need for a formal health plan at school, but the IEP team and nurse will be informed should her medical status change.

Mr. Hollis, a teacher, reports that Emma Rose Callahan is able to engage with content related to health and physical education and can independently identify and summarize relevant articles in these areas. He describes her as polite, helpful to other students, and a joy to have in class. He notes the effort Emma Rose puts forth, as well as her engagement in Math support class. Academic weaknesses in math fluency and written expression remain, but she consistently demonstrates effort and participates appropriately.

Previous parent ratings and behavioral questionnaires have documented clinically significant behavioral symptoms for Emma Rose, most pronounced in aggression, conduct problems, atypicality, and adaptive skills. Parents have also noted significant concerns at home in executive functioning, defiance/aggression, and peer relations. Elevated scores in depression, inattention, and somatic complaints were observed across both emotional and functional domains. These profiles are consistent with early parent/teacher and behavioral/clinical measures from her elementary years.

Both parent and teacher input acknowledged clinically significant levels of inattention in home and school settings, consistent with Emma Rose’s ADHD diagnosis. Further shared concerns included depression, somatization, and attention problems as contributing factors to her educational profile.

Emma Rose’s fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Reed, reported that she showed concerns with withdrawal, learning problems, and peer relations, albeit without observation of significant hyperactive behaviors in the school setting. These observations further support previous findings regarding Emma Rose’s attention difficulties, emotional adjustment, and social relations within the classroom environment.

Emma Rose Callahan received a diagnostic assessment at age three, conducted shortly after her adoption. At this initial evaluation, her developmental history was notable for exposure to trauma and significant neglect prior to adoption. Her medical history included alleged intrauterine exposure to methamphetamine, and birth information was limited; it was known only that she weighed 6 lb 4 oz and was born in Hollister, California.

Developmentally, Emma Rose Callahan had met most milestones on time, but walked at 19 months and began talking around age two, indicating delays in speech and language as well as suspected delays in overall cognitive development. At the time of the assessment, she was meeting expected milestones in fine and gross motor skills and was toilet trained during the day (though with frequent accidents). Despite early adversity, it was noted that Emma Rose Callahan had progressed in development since entering the care of her adoptive parents, and age-appropriate communication and motor skills were not an area of concern going forward.

Behavioral findings were a focus of the early assessment. Results from the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) identified clinically significant withdrawal and somatic complaints, with her adoptive mother endorsing concerns related to emotional reactivity and oppositional defiant problems in the borderline range. The assessment described clinically significant issues with somatic complaints, withdrawal, and social development, and suggested that her history of neglect and trauma might be contributing factors.

These prior evaluations documented Emma Rose Callahan’s complex needs and highlighted the interplay between early trauma, disrupted attachment, and developmental delays. The assessment established a baseline for ongoing supports and interventions, noting her progress since adoption but also identifying areas for close monitoring as she continued to grow and develop.

Emma Rose Callahan’s early developmental history as reported by her adoptive mother is notable for exposure to trauma and severe neglect prior to adoption. She was reported to have been removed from her biological parents’ care at 19 months of age due to suspected neglect and was placed in a foster home briefly before joining her adoptive family, who formally adopted her in June 2013. Medical history includes alleged in utero exposure to methamphetamine, though information about birth events is limited apart from a known birth weight of 6 lbs 4 oz and delivery in Hollister, CA. There were no reported hospitalizations, surgeries, or significant illnesses or injuries during early childhood.

Developmentally, Emma Rose achieved some milestones later than peers; she began walking at 19 months and talking around age two, later using sentences at about three years. Early assessments also suggested delays in overall cognitive and language development and she attended a bilingual preschool program. Emma Rose displayed difficulty with sensory processing and had definite differences compared to peers in her responses to sensory input. Her attention to tasks fluctuated, improving with sensory movement breaks. She met age expectations in fine and gross motor skills, and was able to feed and mostly dress herself, aside from fasteners.

Socially and emotionally, her mother reported that Emma Rose separated easily from her in new environments, showed social interest and good eye contact, and communicated using short sentences, although her speech was sometimes unclear. She responded well to praise and reinforcers, but also experienced meltdowns several times weekly that could include aggression (e.g., screaming, hitting furniture). Parent and teacher rating scales reflected clinically significant symptoms in the areas of withdrawal, somatic complaints, emotional reactivity, oppositional defiance, inattention, and social development. Sensory sensitivities, emotional reactivity, and safety issues related to running/escape behaviors were also noted. Emma Rose usually slept well but wore a pull-up at night and was usually dry; she napped daily and occasionally benefited from supports such as a weighted blanket. Behaviorally, significant symptoms were observed at home, including aggression, executive functioning difficulties, and struggles with peer relationships.

Emma Rose Callahan attended several schools, including a Chinese/English bilingual preschool, Oak Meadow School (residence school), and Creekside Oaks. At the time of her fourth grade initial IEP, she was enrolled at Fairhaven and was receiving Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) through the Resource Specialist Program. The classroom teacher at that time reported that Emma Rose maintained age-appropriate communication skills, participated fully in PE, and had generally legible handwriting. She had attained most developmental milestones within expected limits, except for later walking (19 months) and talking (about age two).

Academically, Emma Rose functioned in the below average to average range relative to peers. Strengths were seen in oral reading fluency, reading comprehension, early reading skills, spelling, essay composition, and numerical operations. Below average performance was noted for math problem solving and math fluency in addition and subtraction. She showed inconsistent performance with multi-step word problems. Written responses often included fragmented or run-on sentences and errors in grammar, mechanics, and spelling.

Behaviorally, the classroom teacher noted ongoing challenges with attending to instruction, following class standards, following directions, and peer interactions. Attention deficits related to ADHD affected her engagement, and teacher/parent rating scales echoed clinically significant concerns in attention, depression, withdrawal, and peer relations. However, she completed classroom testing cooperatively and was able to finish all subtests that were presented. Emma Rose received a combination of general education and special education supports, including short-term counseling and frequent check-ins to support self-regulation and transitions.

blocks.prose:
During interview and direct assessment, Emma Rose Callahan presented as a cooperative and persistent student, able to complete challenging tasks despite complaining about difficulty or making errors. She showed a sense of humor and could laugh at herself when things were hard. She described herself as working slowly and carefully, with good stamina, and shared that she listens and practices repeatedly until she gets words right. In reading aloud, her voice was described as flat in tone, though her pace was otherwise normal. Eye contact was quiet and intermittent.

Emma Rose acknowledged challenges with attention, sometimes acting cautiously but also described self-correcting after impulsivity or errors, and recognized her difficulties with math. She associated successful completion of tasks and better focus with being medicated, sharing, “Without meds it’s really hard, with meds it’s fine.” Emma Rose also described her enjoyment of writing, particularly using metaphors and composing thoughtful essays. She expressed interest in public speaking and noted her self-confidence, but reported a personal dislike for math.

She reported a recent medical improvement after having her tonsils out, which resolved sleep apnea. She also identified herself as a student in a homeschool setting (Options for Youth), and described working through math readiness packets for Math 1.

Emma Rose Callahan is currently a ninth-grade student enrolled at Ridgeway High School, receiving instruction within the Ridgeway-Cordova SELPA. She has an IEP in place for a primary eligibility of Specific Learning Disability (SLD) and receives specialized academic instruction in both English and Math, as well as Study Skills (258 minutes per week), college and career awareness, and general education with accommodations. Areas of academic weakness persist in math fluency, written language, and numerical operations. Math reasoning and multi-step problem solving are further areas of goal focus, with recent assessments indicating a diagnostic score near the 18th percentile and more specific weaknesses in Algebra & Expressions, Fractions & Ratios, Geometry, Measurement/Data/Statistics, and Numbers & Operations.

Her written expression is characterized as an area of weakness, yet she has strengths as a writer and positive performance when supported with structure. For example, she has recently written a two-paragraph expository essay with 75% accuracy and regularly finds and summarizes articles in health and physical education. She has shown growth with the use of graphic organizers and specific writing prompts. Her performance in writing and research is sometimes described as above standard, and she is currently reading at a 7th grade level. Math and written expression, as well as transition skills, remain targeted areas for IEP goals and instruction.

Emma Rose takes multiple medications, including for hypothyroid, bipolar disorder, and ADHD, and is being assisted to find the right dosages. She has no known allergies aside from seasonal ones, and does not require a current health plan. She had her appendix removed in recent years and recovered without difficulty. She continues to be monitored for sleep issues and is scheduled for a CPAP fitting and a summer sleep study due to previous sleep problems. At the beginning of the current school year, Emma Rose frequently fell asleep in class, but with interventions (e.g., breaks, hydrating) she has improved. Mom notes she is shy, which impacts her ability to ask for help, but overall she does not display behaviors that impede her learning. She is polite, helps others, and is regarded as a pleasure to have in class.

Emma Rose’s mother reports she is sensitive to noise and touch and has a documented history of ADHD and Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD). Ongoing sleep problems have been a challenge and are currently being addressed through a forthcoming CPAP evaluation. Medication regimens for ADHD, mood, and thyroid have been implemented with ongoing adjustments. Emma Rose is described as generally compliant and cooperative at home and in school, with strengths in daily living and self-care tasks, though focus and self-regulation remain points of support through both home and school interventions.

Mr. Hollis, one of Emma Rose Callahan’s teachers, highlighted her ability to identify health and physical education topics, locate related articles, and summarize them. He notes her engagement and effort in class, specifically in math support where she is polite, engaged, and a positive presence. Academic support strategies include reinforcement of self-advocacy and engagement in class assignments.

Parental reports across the years indicate a range of clinically significant behavioral symptoms, including aggression, conduct problems, atypical behaviors, and adaptive skill concerns. Parent rating scales and interviews point to alternating episodes of defiance, aggression, depression, and withdrawal, along with challenges in peer relations and executive functioning. Both home and school inputs from previous years highlight sustained inattention, emotional reactivity, and challenges with somatic complaints and self-regulation, all of which have informed the development of school-based supports and therapeutic interventions.

Both parent and teacher share ongoing concerns about Emma Rose’s inattention, depression, and somatic complaints. These concerns have been present across settings and time and are particularly evident in relation to schoolwork and social engagement. Rating scales completed by both reinforce the need for continued support in these areas, as well as for self-regulation and coping strategies.

Teacher ratings and comments, such as from Mrs. Reed, describe concerns regarding withdrawal, learning difficulties, and peer relations. These concerns have not included significant hyperactive behavior within the school setting. Academic and behavioral observations underline Emma Rose’s need for continued support with focus, peer interaction, on-task behavior, and self-regulation.

blocks.prose:
Emma Rose Callahan’s early history is notable for exposure to significant trauma and neglect prior to adoption. She was removed from her biological parents’ care due to severe neglect, experiencing suspected trauma prior to 19 months of age. After a brief period in a foster home, she was placed with her adoptive family, who formally adopted her when she was three. Her early developmental history also included suspected in utero exposure to methamphetamines, but her birth weight and health were otherwise unremarkable, with no major hospitalizations, surgeries, or allergies reported at that time. Emma Rose’s early milestones included walking at 19 months and first using sentences around age three, with initial delays in speech and cognitive development suspected by her adoptive mother. She attended a Chinese/English bilingual preschool and was noted to have made developmental gains in her adoptive home. The adoptive mother also reported ongoing behavioral challenges during early childhood, including frequent meltdowns (2–5 times per week), aggression during those episodes, and clinically significant withdrawal, somatic complaints, and emotional reactivity as rated on behavioral checklists. She exhibited attention and executive functioning difficulties, sensitivity to sensory input, and clinically significant struggles in the areas of social development, peer relationships, and adaptive functioning.

The adoptive mother described Emma Rose as generally socially curious and interactive, though she required redirection and benefited from structured praise and reinforcers. She also displayed signs of sensory processing difficulties, including seeking sensory input and emotional reactivity, and required sensory movement breaks to help sustain her attention. Fine and gross motor, as well as many self-care skills, were age-appropriate, although she was only partially toilet trained with occasional accidents at age three and some difficulty with clothing fasteners. The family described safety concerns related to running or escape behaviors during this same period. The adoptive mother noted that Emma Rose slept well during early childhood after an initial period of nightmares, typically sharing a room with her sister, and may benefit from a weighted blanket for grounding at bedtime.

During her initial IEP assessment in fourth grade, Emma Rose Callahan’s classroom teacher indicated that she met developmental milestones on time except for later walking (19 months) and talking (~2 years). The teacher reported that Emma Rose maintained age-appropriate communication, handwriting, and motor skills, and participated in PE appropriately. The areas flagged for concern were attention to instruction, compliance with class standards, following directions, and peer interactions. The classroom teacher observed average skills in self-care, coping with frustration, attendance, and interactions with staff. Academically, Emma Rose was described as functioning overall in the below average to average range, with strengths highlighted in early reading skills, oral reading fluency, reading comprehension, spelling, and essay composition; however, her math problem solving and certain aspects of math fluency, particularly in addition and subtraction, were notably weaker. She was inconsistent in solving multi-step word problems involving more than one operation, and her writing, while containing areas of relative strength, at times reflected fragmented or run-on sentences, and errors in conventions such as punctuation and grammar.

According to the IEP, she received specialized academic instruction through the Resource Specialist Program (RSP) and short-term counseling support targeting self-regulation and transition. Medically at that time, Emma Rose took prescribed medications (guanfacine, Singulair, melatonin) and had recently undergone an appendectomy without complication. The teacher also noted her shyness and clinically significant levels of inattention in the classroom, consistent with an ADHD diagnosis.

blocks.prose: Emma Rose Callahan shared in interview that medication is a significant support for her daily functioning, stating that “without meds it’s really hard, with meds it’s fine.” She described being homeschooled previously through Options for Youth, and is currently working through math content in preparation for Math 1 using packets. Emma Rose stated that she does not like math but works hard and is careful, although she recognizes that she works more slowly than peers. She shared that in her writing she enjoys creating metaphors and has written essays on profound topics such as life and what happens after death, suggesting creative thinking and reflective interests. She described having self-confidence and expressed interest in public speaking. She reported that in reading aloud she has a flat tone, but her conversational and silent reading pace is typical. She described her cooperative attitude and ability to persist through challenging tasks, sometimes complaining but able to laugh at herself. During testing, she demonstrated intermittent eye contact and was quiet but responsive. She described listening repeatedly to material until getting the words right, suggesting perseverance and self-correction, but noted tendencies toward impulsivity and poor attention at times.

Currently, Emma Rose Callahan is enrolled in ninth grade at Ridgeway High School, participating in a virtual learning setting. She has an active Individualized Education Program (IEP) with a primary classification of Specific Learning Disability (SLD), receiving Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) in both math and study skills alongside some general education coursework with accommodations. Emma Rose also receives college and career awareness services on a monthly basis. Her mother reports that in addition to SLD, Emma Rose has a history of ADHD and Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD), and she manages hypothyroidism with medication. She currently takes Geodon, Trileptal, and Vyvanse. Medical needs are being monitored and do not currently require a health plan, but her mother reports ongoing sleep problems, seasonal allergies, and that Emma Rose is scheduled for a sleep study and CPAP fitting in the near future. Emma Rose had an appendectomy in 2019 and previously had her tonsils removed, which resolved prior sleep apnea.

Emma Rose’s mother identifies academic weaknesses in math fluency/numerical operations and written language, areas which are reflected in assessment data. The diagnostic math score placed her at the 18th national percentile, with notable difficulty in algebra, fractions, geometry, and measurement. Her reading, by contrast, was at a seventh grade level based on diagnostic measures, with above-standard scores in writing research. In class, Emma Rose performs well on summative assessments when supported (e.g., scoring 86%) and can solve one- and two-step equations when given notes and practice. Her mother and teachers agree that Emma Rose puts significant effort into her work, helps classmates, and is polite and engaged, although needs support in transitions, motivation, and goal progress in math and writing. Despite her shyness, which sometimes limits help-seeking, Emma Rose’s day-to-day behavior does not impede learning and is described as cooperative. She continues to receive accommodations and specialized instruction to support her academic growth and successful participation.

Emma Rose's mother further described complex needs reflecting her early experiences and developmental profile, including sensitivity to noise and touch, attention difficulties, and a longstanding diagnosis of ADHD. Sleep problems and seasonal allergies have been ongoing concerns, with Emma Rose receiving medical and educational monitoring for both. Her mother reports that, compared to peers, Emma Rose may be more sensitive to sensory input and prone to difficulties with attention and focus throughout her school history. Academic strengths include reading (currently at a 7th grade level), relative strengths in spelling, and oral reading fluency, with her written language reported as both an area of growth and, at times, a relative strength depending on the specific skill assessed (e.g., essay composition).

Mr. Hollis, a current teacher, noted Emma Rose Callahan’s ability to engage in health and physical education curriculum, highlighting her capacity to research articles and formulate written summaries. He described Emma Rose as polite, engaged, and a joy to teach, further noting that she is willing to help classmates and takes her classwork seriously. While writing remains an area targeted for instructional support, Emma’s interest and participation in class projects and assignments are seen as strengths.

Emma Rose’s parents have described both present and past challenges with behavioral regulation, especially during early childhood, characterized by meltdowns, aggression, withdrawal, and emotional reactivity. Ongoing parent input via rating scales has indicated clinically significant or elevated behaviors related to defiance, aggression, depression, attention, executive functioning, and peer relations, as well as adaptive and conduct problems. Concerns about somatization and atypical behaviors have also been expressed, though at this time her behavior is generally seen as appropriate in the school setting and not interfering with classroom learning. Past and present behavioral and sensory-related issues continue to inform targeted supports at home and in educational settings.

Both parents and previous teachers have consistently reported clinically significant levels of inattention and shared concerns about attention problems, somatization, and depression impacting Emma Rose Callahan both at home and in school. Peer relations and struggles with executive functioning were also noted as ongoing areas of need. While hyperactivity has not been a significant concern in the school environment, these domains continue to be monitored and addressed with support and accommodations.

Teachers, such as Mrs. Reed, reported additional concerns regarding Emma Rose Callahan’s withdrawal, learning problems, and difficulty with peer relationships during her elementary years. Despite the absence of significant hyperactivity observed at school, teachers noted learning and behavioral problems consistent with her complex developmental history and ongoing educational needs.

Emma Rose Callahan's early childhood evaluation, completed at age three, documented a complex developmental and trauma history. Birth information is limited, but it was noted that Emma Rose was born in Hollister, CA, with a birth weight of 6 lb 4 oz. Her medical history included alleged intrauterine exposure to methamphetamine, raising concerns for possible developmental impact. Severe neglect and suspected trauma prior to adoption were reported, including a history of suspected abuse and domestic violence.

At the time of the early assessment, Emma Rose was described as meeting age-appropriate milestones for fine and gross motor skills. She was toilet trained during the day but experienced frequent accidents. Notably, she walked at about 19 months and began talking at about two years, which was somewhat delayed and raised concern for possible overall cognitive and language delays. Findings from the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL) showed clinically significant withdrawal and somatic complaints, with her adoptive mother endorsing concerns in emotional reactivity and oppositional behaviors. The CBCL indicated social development problems and continued concerns in emotional and somatic domains.

It was documented that the history of neglect and exposure to trauma may be contributory to Emma Rose’s developmental challenges. Since entering the care of her adoptive parents, Emma Rose has shown developmental progress. More recently, records indicate she maintains age-appropriate communication skills, participates in physical education with her peers, and demonstrates handwriting within appropriate boundaries.

In summary, previous evaluation findings highlight early exposure to trauma and environmental risk factors, as well as delays in early milestones. However, Emma Rose has demonstrated resilience and growth following adoption and ongoing support.

Emma Rose Callahan’s adoptive mother reports that Emma’s early developmental history is significant for exposure to trauma, including severe neglect prior to her adoption. Emma was removed from her biological parents’ care and placed in foster care for two weeks before joining her adoptive family at 19 months of age, with the legal adoption finalized in June 2013. Her birth history is largely unknown except for a birth weight of 6 lb 4 oz in Hollister, CA, and she is suspected to have had intrauterine exposure to methamphetamine. Emma was delayed in her motor and language milestones, walking at 19 months and talking around age two. Early assessments indicated delays in speech, language, and overall cognitive development, as well as possible sensory integration differences. 

Emma slept well at home, sharing a room with her sister, with no reported nightmares. She has not had significant hospitalizations, surgeries, or illnesses other than routine childhood needs, and she does not have notable allergies. Her adoptive mother describes Emma as able to dress herself (except for managing buttons), feed herself, and generally meet most age-appropriate self-care skills. While Emma has shown steady developmental progress since being in the care of her adoptive parents, her early history of neglect, trauma, and in utero exposure are thought to contribute to ongoing challenges with emotional regulation, attention, and social development. 

The adoptive mother notes that Emma experiences meltdowns 2-5 times per week, with periods of aggression and difficulty being consoled. Sensory processing difficulties are also present, as evidenced by differences in response to sensory input compared to peers. Parent report and behavior inventories from early childhood identified clinically significant withdrawal, somatic complaints, emotional reactivity, and oppositional defiant behaviors, as well as signs of inattention and executive functioning difficulties. Emma’s mother notes that sensory movement breaks help Emma sustain her attention, and weighted blankets at night have been beneficial in providing calming sensory input.

During her fourth grade initial IEP at Fairhaven, Emma Rose Callahan’s classroom teacher and team described several areas of both strength and concern. At the time, Emma was participating in the general education classroom at Oak Meadow School with some pull-out services provided in the Resource Specialist Program (RSP) for specialized academic instruction. In class, Emma demonstrated age-appropriate skills in communication, motor abilities, and adaptive daily living. However, she had some difficulty with attention to instruction, following class routines, directions, and interacting with peers—which her teacher attributed in part to her diagnosed ADHD.

Academically, Emma was functioning in the below average to average range compared to her peers. She showed relative strengths in basic reading skills, oral reading fluency, reading comprehension, spelling, and simple math computation tasks. She reported 52 correct words per minute for grade-level reading and accurate comprehension for most questions. However, she scored below average in math problem solving and was inconsistent when working on multi-step math tasks requiring multiple operations. Her teacher described her written work as sometimes containing fragmented or run-on sentences, with errors in grammar, punctuation, and spelling. In the classroom, Emma displayed average independence with self-care, staff interaction, and coping with frustration. She was noted to be generally cooperative in testing environments and able to complete all tasks presented to her. Short-term counseling in self-regulation strategies was recommended as an IEP service at the time.

blocks.prose:
Emma Rose Callahan was interviewed as part of the evaluation process. She reported that school is much more manageable when she has her medication; without it, she finds things “really hard.” She has a history of medical interventions, including a successful tonsillectomy that resolved previous sleep apnea. Emma currently attends Ridgeway High School (as of ninth grade), and also has experience in a home school model (Options for Youth). Her academic supports focus on math readiness and written tasks, such as preparing for Math 1 and completing assignments in packets.

Emma describes herself as hard-working, noting that she works slowly and carefully, with good stamina. She enjoys writing, especially using metaphors and exploring creative themes, and mentioned writing an essay about life and death. She feels she might be good at public speaking, and is diligent about practicing until she gets things right. However, she does not like math and identifies it as an area of low self-confidence. During assessment, Emma demonstrated a cooperative attitude and persistence, occasionally making errors due to lapses in attention but typically catching and correcting them, sometimes with humor. Her eye contact was intermittent, and her tone of voice could be flat when reading aloud, but her pace of speech was normal in conversation. Overall, Emma presents as thoughtful, cautious, and able to self-correct, though she is sometimes impulsive.

Emma Rose Callahan is currently in ninth grade and attends Ridgeway High School (RIDGEWAY-CORDOVA SELPA). She attends classes with accommodations as outlined in her Individualized Education Program (IEP), and has support through Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) for math and study skills, with additional services for college and career awareness. Emma also began her high school career with SAI support in English. Her mother describes Emma as having good attendance and being able to follow directions, though her shyness sometimes gets in the way of asking for help.

Academically, Emma demonstrates areas of weakness in math fluency, numerical operations, and written expression, with math and writing goals established in her IEP. Her reading skills are reported at a seventh-grade level, with strengths in writing/research, but there is a need for continued support in composing essays and solving multi-step math problems. Diagnostic scores indicate that Emma is performing below the national average in several math benchmarks and in certain aspects of language and vocabulary. Math fluency, written expression, and transition skills are identified as ongoing areas of need. Despite these challenges, Emma has demonstrated improvement with support—her last summative assessment score was 86%, and her two-paragraph essay writing accuracy was at 75% by May 2024. 

Emma has several medical needs, including a diagnosis of hypothyroid, for which she is adjusting her medication. She also takes prescribed medications including Geodon, Trileptal, and Vyvanse. She is not known to have allergies and does not require a health plan at this time, but her mother will inform the school team if this changes. Emma has a history of sleep problems, and is scheduled for a CPAP machine and a sleep study over the summer. The IEP team has identified her as eligible for an Alternative Pathway to a Diploma.

Emma’s mother adds that Emma has a history of both ADHD and Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD), likely related to her complex early history, including adoption at 19 months and in utero exposure to substances. Sensitivity to noise and touch is observed, along with sleep difficulties and seasonal allergies. Emma requires structured supports and reminders to remain engaged in academic and social activities. Her mother observes that, though Emma may seem withdrawn or inattentive at times, she benefits from predictable routines, targeted academic support, and sensory accommodations, particularly for attention and regulation.

Mr. Hollis, who teaches Emma Rose Callahan's Health and PE class, reports that Emma is able to find health-related articles and write summaries about them, suggesting that she can organize information and compose short written pieces when provided with clear expectations.

Parent-completed rating scales and interviews in the past have identified clinically significant behavioral symptoms at home, including aggression, conduct concerns, and atypical behavior. There are also ongoing challenges in executive functioning (such as maintaining routines or completing tasks), as well as peer relationships. Parents endorse very elevated levels of behavior consistent with depression (across emotional and functional domains), and concern for somatic symptoms (such as withdrawal, complaints of physical discomfort, and low energy). Defiant behaviors, inattention, and difficulty with regulation are also noted, contributing to academic and social stressors.

Both parent and teacher report clinically significant levels of inattention in both home and school settings, consistent with Emma's ADHD diagnosis. Shared concerns are present in the areas of depression, somatization (physical symptoms stemming from emotional distress), and difficulties with attention. Emma can struggle with following classroom routines and sustaining engagement if attention wanes, but benefits from sensory movement breaks and frequent redirection.

Emma Rose Callahan’s teachers have observed concerns related to withdrawal and peer relationships in classroom settings, with some evidence of learning and attention problems. However, significant hyperactivity has not been noted at school. Teachers have also remarked that Emma puts effort into her classwork, is polite, and helps other students. Areas of academic strength include reading, spelling, and basic math fluency, but writing may include error patterns typical for her age, and multi-step math reasoning remains less consistent. Teachers recommend a combination of academic support, self-regulation counseling, and accommodations to help Emma access the curriculum and participate successfully.

Emma Rose Callahan received a comprehensive early childhood diagnostic assessment at age three. At the time, her developmental history was significant for exposure to trauma, including suspected neglect and alleged intrauterine exposure to methamphetamine. Information about her birth was limited; it was reported she was born in Hollister, CA, with a birth weight of 6 lb 4 oz. Prior to adoption, severe neglect was documented and considered a possible contributor to her developmental profile.

During the assessment, Emma Rose was noted to have met most developmental milestones on time, though she began walking at 19 months and talking at about two years old. Early concerns were identified regarding delays in speech, language, and suspected overall cognitive development; however, she was meeting milestones for fine and gross motor skills consistent with her age. She was toilet trained during the day but experienced frequent accidents.

Behavioral rating scales completed by her adoptive mother indicated clinically significant withdrawal and somatic complaints. Additionally, Emma scored in the borderline clinical range for emotional reactivity and oppositional defiant concerns, and was rated in the clinically significant range for somatic complaints, withdrawal, and social development problems. These findings were attributed in part to her history of neglect and trauma.

Since coming into the care of her adoptive parents, Emma Rose Callahan has demonstrated developmental progress across domains. Notably, at the time of evaluation, there were no significant concerns noted in communication or motor development, and she participated successfully in physical education with peers. Her handwriting was described as typically legible and within age-appropriate boundaries.

blocks.prose:
Emma Rose Callahan's adoptive mother provided a detailed developmental, medical, and early history. Emma Rose was removed from her biological parents' care due to severe neglect and possible trauma and was adopted by her current family at 19 months of age, following a short foster placement. There is a history of significant early environmental risk including alleged in utero exposure to methamphetamines, and suspected delays in overall cognitive and language development. She began walking at 19 months and talking at about age two, using short sentences by age three. Early assessments indicated delays in speech/language and cognitive growth, as well as clinically significant emotional and behavioral symptoms, including aggression during meltdowns, withdrawal, somatic complaints, sensory processing difficulties, and frequent inattention. At age 3, she was attending a bilingual Chinese/English preschool and had shown progress in developmental skills such as self-care, feeding with utensils, and managing basic dressing tasks aside from fasteners.

Emma Rose slept well at night, generally took naps daily, and benefited from sensory accommodations including movement breaks and potential use of a weighted blanket to help with regulation. She demonstrated safety risks associated with running/escape and showed definite sensory-seeking and emotional reactivity compared to her peers. No significant medical illnesses, surgeries, or allergies were reported in early childhood.

Parent rating scales and checklists indicated ongoing challenges with attention, anxiety, aggression/oppositionality, social withdrawal, and adaptive skills. Emma's mother reported that she benefited from structure, positive reinforcement, and patient redirection to remain on task or self-regulate emotionally. Emma separated from her mother easily, interacted socially with peers and staff, and could communicate with short sentences, although her speech clarity varied. While these early challenges were significant, Emma Rose Callahan has made progress in her development and adjustment since her adoption.

Emma Rose Callahan's classroom teachers throughout elementary and early middle school have described her as maintaining age-expected communication, gross and fine motor, and daily living skills, with legible handwriting and satisfactory participation in PE activities. She met most developmental milestones, except for later walking and talking, and was not noted to have significant medical issues beyond a recent appendectomy. Emma Rose has received Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) and Resource Specialist Program (RSP) support and short-term counseling for regulation strategies, reflecting complex academic and emotional needs. Teachers noted that Emma Rose displayed average independence in self-care, staff interactions, and coping with frustration, but experienced persistent difficulties with paying attention to instruction, following class routines, managing peer interactions, and following directions, often linked to her diagnosis of ADHD.

Academically, Emma Rose functioned at a below average to average level when compared to her peers. She demonstrated strengths in basic early reading, phonics, fluency, spelling, and essay composition, but weaknesses in reading comprehension, essay and paragraph structure, and, notably, math fluency and word problem-solving. Math operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication within 100) were areas of relative strength, but multi-step reasoning or problems involving unfamiliar formats were less consistent. Teachers also described strengths in oral reading rate and accuracy, with comprehension performance ranging 70–75% (mostly with supports in place). Writing samples were often fragmented, with errors in grammar, punctuation, and conventions, though Emma was able to express ideas when given structure and time.

Attention difficulties associated with ADHD were frequently cited as impacting Emma's engagement and focus in the classroom. Both rating scales and observation data reported significant inattention, emotional reactivity, and occasional withdrawal or oppositionality, though classic hyperactivity symptoms were not prominent in the school setting. Teachers observed that Emma benefited from direct support, clear routines, and individualized accommodations.

blocks.display_label: Student/Client/Patient Input — Student profile and interview
blocks.prose:
Emma Rose Callahan expressed insight into her learning profile and coping strategies during her interview. She reported that school is much more challenging without her prescribed medication; with medication, she feels she can manage academic demands effectively. Emma identified Math as her least preferred subject, noting ongoing struggles with math fluency and numerical operations, but described engaging with "get ready for Math 1" materials in a packet-based, home school setting.

Emma is proud of her effort and stamina in academics, recognizing that she works slowly and carefully, especially on extended tasks. She noted that she listens to instructions repeatedly until she is confident in her accuracy and feels that this approach has helped her—particularly in areas like writing and language. She described her writing as creative and said she enjoys using metaphors and tackling big questions, such as the meaning of life, indicating her interest in expressive language and conceptual thinking. Emma also shared that she believes she would excel at public speaking, despite generally being shy about asking for help. She described herself as cooperative and persistent, willing to laugh about difficulties and try again.

During assessment, Emma demonstrated a quiet and cautious style, with intermittent eye contact and a flat tone when reading aloud, but was more animated and paced naturally in conversation. She could be impulsive at times but often self-corrected upon review. She acknowledged a long-standing problem with attention, contributing to occasional mistakes in her work. Emma noted improvement in her sleep and alertness after having her tonsils removed, resolving prior sleep apnea. She also described improvements in self-regulation practices, such as using scheduled breaks and movement when tired or frustrated, and was aware of ongoing efforts to address sleep quality and health in partnership with her medical team.

Emma Rose Callahan is currently in 9th grade at Ridgeway High School, receiving instruction through the Ridgeway-Cordova SELPA, with accommodations and an IEP specifying a primary disability of Specific Learning Disability (SLD). The IEP is current, and Emma is supported through Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) in math and study skills (258 minutes per week), general education with additional accommodations, and brief monthly services for college and career awareness.

Her mother reports ongoing weaknesses in math fluency, numerical operations, and written expression, with these designated as primary areas of educational need and formal goals on her IEP. Emma also receives support in transition skills. She presents with a complex health history including ADHD, Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD), hypothyroidism (being managed and monitored for medication adjustment), and seasonal allergies, but currently does not require a separate health plan. Emma is prescribed Geodon, Trileptal, and Vyvanse, the latter noted as critical to maintaining her day-to-day focus and academic stamina. Past sleep problems (falling asleep in morning classes) are being addressed: Emma is undergoing assessment and equipment fitting for a CPAP machine and participating in a sleep study. Her mother appreciates the school's responsiveness to these additional health needs.

Academically, Emma is reading at a 7th grade level and receives ongoing SAI in English and study skills. Diagnostic assessment shows a composite math score at the 18th national percentile (notably below average), with performance breakdowns on algebraic expressions, fractions and ratios, geometry, and other content strands indicating consistent challenges. Writing and research are described as strengths in some assessments, but these skills remain an ongoing area for further improvement per her teachers. More recently, Emma has shown upward trends in summative assessment performance (most recently 86% on a major test) and met benchmark goals for math and writing tasks with supports and accommodations. Despite her challenges, her mother notes that Emma has good attendance, is able to follow directions, is polite and helpful to others, and cares deeply about her grades.

Socially, Emma’s shyness continues to affect her willingness to seek help, but she does not engage in disruptive behaviors and is generally able to function independently with minimal supervision. There are no major behaviors impeding access to learning at this stage. Emma will pursue an alternative pathway to a diploma due to eligibility for the California Alternative Assessment and is currently enrolled in supplementary academic programs, including private placement by parent choice.

Emma Rose Callahan's mother adds that Emma has a longstanding diagnosis of ADHD and demonstrates hypersensitivity to noise and touch. These sensory processing issues, observed since early childhood, occasionally impact Emma’s ability to remain focused and comfortable in busy or noisy environments. In educational contexts, Emma’s mother has advocated for sensory accommodations and consistent routines.

Emma’s mother also offered additional observations about her social-emotional needs: Emma is sensitive, becomes withdrawn in unfamiliar situations, and may require reassurance, proactive check-ins, or scheduled breaks to support regulation. While impulsivity and emotional reactivity have been prominent at various points in her development, improvements have been seen with medication, therapeutic supports, and structured school interventions.

Mr. Hollis, Emma Rose Callahan's physical education and health teacher, reports that Emma is able to access the curriculum through alternative assignments, such as researching health topics and writing summaries. Mr. Hollis notes that Emma successfully completes these tasks when given clear directions and support, demonstrating emerging skills in written expression and the ability to engage in health-related subject areas. He describes her as cooperative and willing to try, even when assignments are new or outside of her comfort zone.

Parent ratings from home settings continue to reflect long-standing behavioral and emotional complexities for Emma Rose Callahan. Parents report clinically significant symptoms of aggression, defiance, and executive functioning challenges, as well as marked struggles with peer relations and occasional adaptive skill deficits. Parents endorsed behaviors reflecting withdrawal, somatic complaints, depression, atypicality, and attention problems. Concerns around inattention are consistently elevated in both home and school environments, aligning with Emma's ADHD diagnosis. Parents and teachers alike noted these concerns, with shared observations around mood variability, somatic complaints, and self-regulation difficulties. Although the degree and manifestation of these symptoms has varied over time, Emma’s family remains vigilant in monitoring her emotional and behavioral well-being and partnering with school teams to provide support.

Parent and teacher input highlights clinically significant levels of inattention in both home and classroom settings. Both parties have shared ongoing concerns related to depression, somatization, and attention regulation. These concerns have shaped Emma’s eligibility for special education supports and guide intervention targets. Executive function challenges, avoidance, and emotional dysregulation—sometimes leading to withdrawal or defiance—have been longstanding and continue to require collaborative problem-solving between school and home.

Teachers report persistent difficulties with peer relations, learning problems, and social withdrawal in the classroom. Mrs. Reed, a classroom teacher, specifically identified these as ongoing areas of concern, noting that Emma may struggle to initiate or sustain social interactions with peers and sometimes appears withdrawn or quiet. Despite these challenges, she is observant and follows routines when cued. Teachers also noted that, while classic hyperactive behaviors are not dominant for Emma in the school environment, her ability to focus and fully engage with academics is impacted by attention and motivation fluctuations. Teachers highlight the need for scaffolded support and structure to promote consistent participation and learning.

Documentation from prior educational records and assessments consistently note ADHD as part of Emma Rose Callahan’s diagnostic profile. Emma Rose Callahan’s adoptive mother provided information regarding Emma’s early developmental and medical background. Emma was exposed to significant trauma and severe neglect prior to adoption, including suspected abuse and a history of in utero methamphetamine exposure. She was removed from her biological parents’ care and placed in foster care for two weeks before joining her current family at 19 months of age, where she was later formally adopted. Medical records indicate her birth weight was 6 lbs 4 oz, but other birth details are limited.

Developmental history noted delays: Emma began walking at 19 months and talking around 2 years old. She attended a Chinese/English bilingual preschool (Sunshine/Bright Start Preschool) and was noted to have delays in speech, language, and overall cognitive development. Despite these early challenges, reports indicate that Emma had made developmental progress in the care of her adoptive parents, meeting many age-appropriate self-care, fine and gross motor milestones by age three, such as dressing herself (except for buttons), feeding herself, and unzipping zippers.

Emma exhibited clinically significant sensory processing difficulties and emotional and behavioral concerns in early childhood. Her adoptive mother described meltdowns two to five times per week, including severe aggression (screaming, hitting furniture), clinically significant withdrawal, emotional reactivity, somatic complaints, and oppositional/defiant problems at home. She showed differences in responding to sensory input compared to peers, with needs for movement breaks and possibly a weighted blanket to help ‘ground’ her at night. Safety concerns related to running/escape behaviors were also reported.

Her medical history at age three included no hospitalizations or major illnesses, and she was not taking medications. Emma had consistent sleep habits and shared a room with her sister, generally sleeping well overnight and napping daily. Toilet training was in progress, but she was not consistently dry. Parental rating scales at that time indicated very elevated symptoms in the areas of depression, somatic complaints, attention problems, anxiety, withdrawal, social developmental problems, aggression, emotional reactivity, and oppositional defiant behaviors.

The adoptive mother consistently emphasized that Emma’s complex history, including exposure to trauma and neglect, contributed to her behavioral and emotional profile.

Emma Rose Callahan’s fourth-grade classroom teacher participated in the initial IEP process, providing insights into her academic and classroom functioning. At that time, Emma was attending Oak Meadow School, with her residence school listed as Creekside Oaks, following attendance at a bilingual preschool setting. An IEP was initiated to support ongoing academic needs.

The teacher reported that Emma maintained age-appropriate skills in communication, gross and fine motor development, and adaptive daily living. Areas not of current concern included her ability to participate in physical education and her handwriting, which was typically legible and within appropriate boundaries. Developmental milestones were met with the exception of walking (at 19 months) and beginning to talk in two-to-three-word sentences around age two to three. Emma was cooperative during testing and completed all assessment tasks presented.

Academically, Emma was reported to function in the below average to average range, with strengths noted in early reading skills, oral reading fluency, reading comprehension, spelling, essay composition, and alphabet writing fluency. Her teacher cited consistent weaknesses in attention to instruction, following class standards and directions, and interactions with peers—particularly those linked to ADHD symptoms. Math presented as an area of need, with strengths in numerical operations but below average performance (inconsistency) with multi-step math problem-solving.

Emma was receiving Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) in the Resource Specialist Program as a pull-out service, as well as short-term counseling with the school psychologist to support her regulation and transition. The teacher noted that Emma demonstrated average skills in self-care, staff interactions, coping with frustration, and attendance. She was described as cooperative and able to be redirected in class.

blocks.prose:
During her student interview, Emma Rose Callahan was self-reflective about her strengths and challenges. She described an ongoing reliance on medication to manage her functioning—"Without meds it’s really hard, with meds it’s fine"—and reported a history of medical procedures, including tonsil removal which alleviated prior sleep apnea. Emma is currently enrolled at Ridgeway High School and mentioned a period of homeschooling through Options for Youth.

Emma described perseverance in her academics, especially in writing, where she enjoys using metaphors and has written essays on abstract topics like life and death. She believes she could excel in public speaking and frequently re-reads or listens to text to ensure accuracy. Math remains her least preferred subject, sometimes motivating her only minimally to complete related work, though she is preparing for Math 1 through instructional packets. Emma characterized herself as hardworking with good stamina, but also notes that she works slowly and carefully.

Observationally, Emma presents as quiet, with intermittent eye contact and a flat tone when reading aloud, though she speaks with a normal pace in conversation. During assessment, she was cooperative and persistent, sometimes complaining about difficult tasks but able to laugh at herself and self-correct when errors occurred. She reported feeling self-conscious about her reading style and being unsure about her attention and impulsivity. In general, she demonstrates good effort but struggles with math, sustained focus, and motivation at times.

Emma’s mother noted that she is currently attending Ridgeway High School and participating in a virtual IEP process through the RIDGEWAY-CORDOVA SELPA. Emma has an IEP in place for a primary disability of Specific Learning Disability (SLD). Her mother reported she is reading at a seventh grade level, according to recent diagnostic results; however, areas of weaker performance include math fluency/numerical operations and written language. Math reasoning and computation are also described as areas requiring ongoing support, with her diagnostic scores ranking at the 18th percentile nationally and current performance in core algebra and number operations well below grade level. Math fluency, written expression, and transition skills are current goal areas.

Emma is enrolled in Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) for Math and Study Skills and receives college and career awareness services monthly. Previously, she came to Fairhaven High with SAI English and Study Skills. Medically, she is working to balance medications for hypothyroidism and is prescribed Geodon, Trileptal, and Vyvanse. Emma also experiences sleep problems, seasonal allergies, and is being fitted for a CPAP machine and will participate in a sleep study over the summer. She had her appendix out in 2019 but recovered without complications.

Her mother noted that Emma can be shy, which at times limits her willingness to seek additional help, but that she generally demonstrates good attendance and motivation. At the start of the year, Emma frequently fell asleep in class during morning periods but has developed strategies (such as taking breaks and drinking water) to remain engaged. Behaviorally, Emma does not present with significant disruptive behaviors and follows directions. Her mother highlighted strengths in helping others, being polite, putting in effort, and taking her classwork seriously.

The IEP team has determined Emma is eligible for an alternative pathway to a diploma, given her participation in the California Alternative Assessment and her current programming. Her anticipated completion date is 2028.

Additional parent input confirms Emma Rose Callahan’s clinical diagnoses of ADHD and Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD), as well as a history of sensitivity to noise and touch. Parent/teacher and parent rating scales have reflected clinically significant behaviors at home and in the school environment, including inattention, struggles with executive functioning, aggression/defiance, depression, somatic symptoms, and difficulties with peer relationships. Previous assessment data highlights significant elevations in withdrawal, somatic complaints, and social development problems. At school, however, significant hyperactivity is not observed, and Emma does not engage in behaviors that impede her learning or that of others.

Mr. Hollis, a current teacher, noted that Emma Rose Callahan is able to engage in written work across subject areas; for example, she can select an article related to health or physical education and compose a summary of its content. This reflects her goal area of written expression, as well as her ability to connect learning to varied classroom contexts.

Parent reports using behavior rating scales highlighted clinically significant symptoms in the areas of aggression, conduct problems, atypicality, adaptive skills, executive functioning, defiance, and peer relations at home. There were also marked elevations in emotional and functional symptoms related to depression. These concerns were most evident in the home setting, with the school environment showing less severe behavioral disruption, particularly in the domains of hyperactivity and impulsivity.

Joint input from parent and teacher emphasized clinically significant levels of inattention in both home and classroom settings, as well as shared concerns about depression, somatization, and ongoing problems with attention. This collaborative perspective highlights Emma’s persistent challenges with maintaining focus and emotional regulation across environments.

Mrs. Reed, a classroom teacher, provided additional observations noting elevated concerns in areas of withdrawal, learning problems, and peer relations. She reiterated that while hyperactive behaviors are not present at school, Emma does demonstrate learning difficulties and some social withdrawal in the classroom. These insights align with parent reports and formal rating scales.

Emma Rose Callahan’s adoptive mother provided a detailed developmental and medical history. Emma was removed from her biological parents’ care due to suspected severe neglect and trauma, with alleged in utero exposure to methamphetamine. She was placed in foster care and then with her adoptive family at 19 months, and was formally adopted in June 2013. Birth history details are limited but indicate a birth weight of 6 lb 4 oz.

Developmental milestones were delayed: Emma walked at about 19 months and began talking at about 2 years, using sentences by age 3. Early assessments noted delays in speech, language, and suspected delays in overall cognitive development. Emma attended the Sunshine Bilingual Chinese/English preschool and later continued in a similar bilingual program.

Emma had no significant medical hospitalizations, illnesses, or surgeries in early childhood, and did not require regular medication or have known allergies at that time. Her sleep patterns were typical for her age; she shared a room with her sister, fell asleep within 20–30 minutes, and slept through the night. She napped daily for 1–2.5 hours, slept in a pull-up but was typically dry, and was nearly fully toilet trained with occasional accidents.

Emma’s adoptive mother reported progress in developmental domains since joining her current family. Fine motor, gross motor, and many age-appropriate self-care skills (including dressing, feeding, and managing simple tasks) were within expected ranges, with difficulty only on complex fasteners like buttons.

Notably, Emma showed significant sensory processing differences, including sensitivity to noise and touch, and benefited from sensory movement breaks during activities to sustain attention. She demonstrated sensory-seeking behaviors and at times had challenges sustaining attention, especially when her arousal level was low.

Behaviors of concern included frequent meltdowns (2–5 times weekly, sometimes involving aggression toward furniture), severe aggression during meltdowns, and difficulty being consoled. Parent and clinical rating scales from that period showed clinically significant or borderline clinical symptoms relating to withdrawal, somatic complaints, emotional reactivity, inattention, anxiety, aggression, oppositionality, and social problems. Parent reports also indicated clinically significant symptoms of atypicality, aggression, depression, conduct and adaptive skill concerns, defiance, struggles with peer relations, and sensory sensitivities. Despite these challenges, Emma was described as socially interested, able to separate from her mother, make eye contact, and initiate social play with peers and adults.

Emma Rose Callahan’s fourth grade classroom teacher described her as presenting an average skill set for her age in the areas of independence in self-care, interactions with staff, coping with frustration, attendance, and communication. Her handwriting was typically legible, and her gross and fine motor skills were within age expectations. No significant difficulties were noted in her participation in PE or her communication skills.

Academic assessment showed Emma functioning within the below average to average range compared to grade-level peers. Reading and spelling were relative strengths, with performance in oral reading fluency, comprehension, and essay composition at or near grade level. However, she demonstrated weaknesses in math problem-solving, with inconsistent accuracy when solving multi-step word problems, especially with more than one operation. Emma successfully added, subtracted, and multiplied within 100 at high accuracy rates, but showed below average scores in other numerical operations and math fluency activities involving addition and subtraction. Written responses sometimes contained errors in sentence structure, punctuation, and grammar.

Behaviorally, the teacher noted some ongoing concerns with attention to instruction, following directions and class standards, and peer interactions, suggesting challenges consistent with her known diagnosis of ADHD. Nonetheless, Emma was described as cooperative during assessments and able to complete required tasks. She met most developmental milestones on time except for walking and talking, which were slightly delayed.

blocks.prose:
During her interview, Emma Rose Callahan described herself as quiet and cooperative, with intermittent eye contact during conversation. She reported that focusing on schoolwork is much harder without medication but manageable when she takes it. Emma reflected on her medical history, noting that having her tonsils out eliminated previous sleep apnea. Sleep remains a focus, as she is being evaluated for a CPAP device and will participate in a sleep study over the summer. She mentioned a period of falling asleep in class and recent improvements in staying awake.

Emma is enrolled at Options for Youth for home-based instruction and receives math prep packets aimed at readying her for Math 1. She described her approach to learning as persistent—listening repeatedly until she masters material and working slowly and carefully. In reading, she has a flat tone when reading aloud but a normal pace in other settings. She expressed confidence in her stamina and work ethic.

Writing is an area where Emma takes pride; she enjoys using metaphors and has written essays on philosophical topics. She believes she would excel at public speaking. At the same time, Emma reported she does not like math, has low self-confidence in that subject, and must work especially hard. She noted that she sometimes acts impulsively but is able to self-correct, and she could laugh at herself even during challenging moments.

Emma Rose Callahan is a ninth grade student at Ridgeway High School, with an IEP in place under the category of Specific Learning Disability. She previously received SAI English and Study Skills support at Fairhaven and now receives Specialized Academic Instruction for Math and Study Skills, along with supports in college and career awareness. Mom reported academic weaknesses in math fluency, numerical operations, and written language, which are reflected in diagnostic data (e.g., a math score in the 18th national percentile) and classroom observations. Emma is working on multi-step linear equations and expository writing with scaffolded support.

Emma has hypothyroidism, for which her team is adjusting medication, as well as diagnoses of ADHD and Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD). She currently takes Geodon, Trileptal, and Vyvanse, and also reported a history of sleep problems for which she is now being evaluated and may start CPAP therapy. Medical history also includes previous surgery for appendicitis and ongoing seasonal allergies.

Her mother notes that Emma has good attendance, follows directions, but is shy—which can limit her help-seeking behavior. Emma does not have behaviors that currently impede learning, and there are no concerning behaviors that require a special plan. In the classroom, Emma strives to do her best, cares about her grades, and helps her peers.

Her reading is at a seventh-grade level, but vocabulary achievement is somewhat lower. Challenges persist in math fluency, written expression, and transitions. She continues to receive general education with accommodations and targeted interventions within her IEP, including resource support and short-term counseling for coping and self-regulation.

Emma’s mother (in addition to the above) reported that Emma shows sensitivity to noise and touch, reflective of ongoing sensory processing difficulties noted in prior evaluations. She has a long-standing history of ADHD, which has impacted focus and engagement both at home and in the classroom. Sleep problems have been a recurring concern, as have periods of inattention and apparent sensory seeking. Interventions such as movement breaks, consistent routines, and environmental adjustments continue to be necessary for her ongoing success.

Mr. Hollis, Emma’s teacher in health and PE, shared that Emma Rose Callahan can find and summarize articles related to health and physical education, indicating she can engage in integrated written expression tasks when provided with a clear framework. This aligns with her overall performance in writing with structured support.

Emma’s caregivers and parents, as reported in past and current assessments, have noted both progress and ongoing concerns. Past assessments highlighted frequent meltdowns and episodes of aggression, sometimes associated with attempts at task demand or transitions. Parents reported clinically significant symptoms relating to depression, anxiety, attention, aggression, conduct, withdrawal, atypicality, and adaptive skills. Ratings by both parents and teachers consistently pointed to high levels of inattention across settings (home and school), struggles with peer relationships, and executive functioning challenges. Over time, there have also been improvements in daily living skills, self-care, dress/undress abilities, and social interest, but support remains necessary in transitions, behavioral regulation, and sensory processing.

Feedback from parent-teacher input reflected clinically significant levels of inattention and shared concerns about depression, somatization, and attention problems. Both home and classroom settings revealed similar patterns of challenges related to inattention, emotional reactivity, and mood. Teachers additionally noted long-standing concerns around withdrawal, peer relations, and learning problems, though no clinically significant hyperactive behaviors were evident in the school setting. Interventions or accommodations are generally needed to support Emma’s engagement, focus, and emotional stability.

School staff, including Mrs. Reed and other team members, have reported concerns in the areas of withdrawal, peer relations, attention to instruction, and learning problems. Emma’s skills with adults are age-appropriate, but she continues to need adult prompting and redirection at times. Academically, she performs at levels ranging from below average to average, with ongoing strengths in reading and notable challenges in written expression and multi-step math reasoning. Her work habits, while careful and persistent, are affected by attentional lapses. Overall, the team describes her as cooperative, a positive presence, and willing to work through difficult moments with support.

Math assessment scores revealed relative strength in numerical operations (addition within 100 at 93% accuracy, subtraction at 83%, and multiplication at 88%), but she was inconsistent with multi-step word problems and below average in math problem solving and addition/subtraction fluency. Diagnostic results place her at the 18th national percentile in numerical operations, with academic weaknesses in math fluency, math reasoning, and written language. On a math skills assessment, Emma scored 3/11 in Algebra & Expressions, Fractions & Ratios, and Geometry; 1/11 in Measurement, Data & Statistics; and 5/11 in Numbers & Operations. Her most recent summative math assessment result was 86%. Reading skills reflect a seventh-grade reading level, performance of 8/15 in both Reading Literature and Informational Text, and 5/14 in Language and Vocabulary; she received 15/25 on a recent vocabulary quiz.

Emma has continued to develop her written expression. She is able to write a paragraph or a two-paragraph expository essay with emerging topic sentences, supporting statements, and summary conclusions at 70–75% accuracy. Her writing style includes the use of metaphors, and she enjoys topics across health and physical education, with capacity to find articles and write summaries. Emma reports confidence in her writing and believes she might excel at public speaking, though she does not like math.

Emma's experience reflects engagement with the curriculum, consistent attendance, and ongoing academic challenges primarily in math fluency, written expression, and transition skills. She utilizes repetition and practice to improve skills, as shared through her own interview responses.

**Intervention:**
Emma receives interventions to address her areas of need in math, written expression, and transition. At Ridgeway High School, she has Specialized Academic Instruction (SAI) in Study Skills for 258 weekly minutes, along with college and career awareness services for 15 minutes monthly each. Academic support includes pull-out SAI provided through the Resource Specialist Program (RSP) and accommodations in general education classes.

Historically, Emma received SAI in math, with services delivered in a small group or RSP setting for 240 weekly minutes during elementary school. To ease her transition in fourth grade, she participated in brief counseling with the school psychologist/counselor, focusing on self-regulation and coping strategies, meeting twice monthly for 30 minutes each over a six-month period. Her fine and gross motor skills were both considered age-appropriate, and she was toilet trained during the day albeit with frequent accidents.
