blocks.prose: Emma Rose Callahan described herself as a hardworking and persistent student who puts considerable effort into her work. She expressed that medication significantly helps her manage attention and learning challenges, saying, “Without meds it’s really hard, with meds it’s fine.” She described her history of sleep issues, noting, “I had my tonsil out and no more sleep apnea,” and ongoing efforts to address sleep and energy concerns through a CPAP and sleep study. Emma Rose currently attends Options for Youth (a home school program) and is preparing for high school Math 1 using packet-based curriculum. She recognized math as especially challenging and voiced her dislike for the subject, but continues to work through her assignments. In writing, Emma Rose finds meaning in creative expression and enjoys using metaphors, sharing that she wrote an essay about life and what happens when we die. She takes a careful and repetitive approach to mastering language, stating, “I listen over and over till I get the words right,” and believes she would excel in public speaking. She characterized herself as diligent and careful, albeit slow in her work. During interview, Emma Rose displayed flat tone when reading aloud but spoke at a normal pace conversationally, gave intermittent eye contact, and was generally cooperative—displaying persistence and humor about challenging tasks. Attention was described as cautious but sometimes impulsive, often self-correcting, with occasional errors linked to inattention.

Emma Rose’s mother provided updated information on her current high school status and educational planning. Emma Rose is enrolled at Ridgeway High School with an Individualized Education Program (IEP) in place for a primary eligibility of Specific Learning Disability (SLD). She continues to receive Specialized Academic Instruction in math, English, and study skills along with general education accommodations, college and career awareness, and support in study skills. Recent diagnostic testing placed her in the 18th national percentile overall, with her reading at approximately a 7th-grade level. Areas of strength include reading comprehension and essay writing, while persistent weaknesses are noted in math fluency, numerical operations, written language, and transition skills. Emma Rose has current medical diagnoses of hypothyroidism (with ongoing adjustment of medication doses), ADHD, and Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD), and takes Geodon, Trileptal, and Vyvanse. While she has a history of hospitalizations for tonsil and appendix removal, she currently reports good health with no significant ongoing issues other than seasonal allergies and some sleep challenges (with a sleep study and CPAP fitting pending). Her mother reported that Emma Rose cares about her grades, attends class regularly, is able to follow directions, and is described as shy, which at times affects her willingness to seek help. She is reported to not have behavioral concerns that impede learning, although there were previous sleep problems causing her to fall asleep in class—these are now managed with strategies like scheduled breaks.

Additional parental input confirmed that Emma Rose continues to exhibit sensitivity to noise and touch, consistent with her longstanding sensory processing difficulties. Her mother specifically described ongoing struggles with attention and distractibility, reporting that these challenges are significant enough to affect Emma’s daily functioning at both home and school and are consistent with a diagnosis of ADHD.

Mr. Hollis, a teacher familiar with Emma Rose in the area of health and physical education, noted that she is able to locate and summarize health-related articles, pointing to her ability to comprehend, organize, and express ideas in writing with appropriate support.

Parent rating scales and reports identified clinically significant behavior symptoms related to aggression and conduct problems, with further concerns regarding atypicality and adaptive skill development. Emma Rose’s parent described very elevated behaviors associated with depression, executive function deficits, and defiance/aggression, as well as social challenges including peer relations. Other concerns included somatization, attention problems, and home-based difficulties with adaptive skills.

Both parent and teacher sources emphasized clinically significant levels of inattention across settings, frequent concerns with depression and somatic symptoms, and ongoing challenges related to attention and motivation. The team also noted some positive patterns, such as Emma Rose’s ability to complete academic tasks when engaged and her appropriate interactions with staff and in vocational or adaptive living domains.

School personnel, including Mrs. Reed, reported persistent concerns in the areas of withdrawal, learning problems, and peer relationships. However, significant problems with hyperactivity were not observed in the school setting. Teachers recognized Emma Rose’s challenges with attention, compliance with class expectations, and forming peer connections, but also observed average skills in many functional and adaptive domains and improvement in written communication and classroom participation with support.

She was born in Hollister, California, with a birth weight of 6 pounds 4 ounces; reported medical history includes alleged intrauterine exposure to methamphetamine. Early assessments and subsequent records indicate a history of severe neglect before adoption, with trauma suspected including possible abuse and environmental deprivation. Her communication skills and handwriting are within expected boundaries for her grade and age.

She is diagnosed with hypothyroidism and takes medication; her parents and physicians are working together to determine and adjust the proper dosage. Her ability to manage sleep and mood symptoms has improved notably with medication, with Emma indicating she is able to function well with medications. No other major hospitalizations, surgeries, or injuries are reported.

Emma Rose Callahan's early developmental history is notable for exposure to significant trauma and severe neglect prior to adoption. Early assessment indicated delays in speech and language development and suspected delays in overall cognitive development. She was walking at 19 months and began talking around age 2, with early sentences at about age 3. In preschool, she attended a bilingual Chinese/English program. Her sleep was described as typical for age (sleeping through the night, napping during the day) with some lingering difficulties around sleep onset. The adoptive mother noted that Emma Rose benefited from sensory movement breaks to sustain her attention and suggested a weighted blanket might help her sleep. At age three, no hospitalizations or major illnesses had occurred, and she was not taking medications.

In fourth grade at Oak Meadow School, with initial IEP services initiated at Fairhaven, Emma Rose Callahan was noted by her teacher as maintaining communication and handwriting skills within age expectations, and not showing concern in motor skills or PE participation. Her academic functioning ranged from below average to average relative to peers, with Early Reading Skills, Word Reading, Oral Reading Fluency, Reading Comprehension, Spelling, and Essay Composition as areas of relative strength. Numerical Operations presented relative strength, though areas of weakness included math word problems and calculation fluency (e.g., some inconsistencies in multi-step operations). Written responses were sometimes marked by errors (run-on or fragmented sentences, issues with capitalization, punctuation, spelling, and subject/verb agreement). Emma Rose demonstrated attention deficits associated with ADHD, affecting engagement and focus in class; her teacher observed difficulties with attention to instruction, following directions and class standards, as well as interacting with peers. However, her self-care, interactions with staff, coping with frustration, attendance, and punctuality were considered average. Testing observations noted Emma Rose was cooperative and able to complete all tasks presented. At that time, SAI services were provided for 240 minutes weekly in a resource setting, and short-term counseling continued to support self-regulation. Information on early development confirmed milestone attainment except for delays in walking and talking.

blocks.prose: Emma Rose Callahan's early developmental history is notable for exposure to significant trauma and severe neglect prior to adoption. She was reportedly exposed to methamphetamine in utero and removed from her biological parents at 19 months, spending two weeks in foster care before joining her adoptive family and being formally adopted in June 2013. Early assessment indicated delays in speech and language development and suspected delays in overall cognitive development. She was walking at 19 months and began talking around age 2, with early sentences at about age 3. In preschool, she attended a bilingual Chinese/English program. Her adoptive mother reported clinically significant behavioral symptoms, including meltdowns 2–5 times per week involving aggression toward furniture and difficulty consoling; findings were corroborated by behavior checklists showing clinically significant withdrawal, somatic complaints, and social developmental problems, as well as borderline clinical scores in emotional reactivity and oppositional defiant problems. Sensory processing difficulties and clear differences from peers’ responses to sensory input were present, along with safety concerns due to running behaviors and escape attempts. At that time, Emma Rose demonstrated age-appropriate fine and gross motor skills, was able to feed and mostly dress herself (with support for fasteners), and had emerging self-care skills. Her sleep was described as typical for age (sleeping through the night, napping during the day) with some lingering difficulties around sleep onset. The adoptive mother noted that Emma Rose benefited from sensory movement breaks to sustain her attention and suggested a weighted blanket might help her sleep. At age three, no hospitalizations or major illnesses had occurred, and she was not taking medications.

In fourth grade at Oak Meadow School, with initial IEP services initiated at Fairhaven, Emma Rose Callahan was noted by her teacher as maintaining communication and handwriting skills within age expectations, and not showing concern in motor skills or PE participation. Her academic functioning ranged from below average to average relative to peers, with Early Reading Skills, Word Reading, Oral Reading Fluency, Reading Comprehension, Spelling, and Essay Composition as areas of relative strength. Numerical Operations presented relative strength, though areas of weakness included math word problems and calculation fluency (e.g., some inconsistencies in multi-step operations). Written responses were sometimes marked by errors (run-on or fragmented sentences, issues with capitalization, punctuation, spelling, and subject/verb agreement). Emma Rose demonstrated attention deficits associated with ADHD, affecting engagement and focus in class; her teacher observed difficulties with attention to instruction, following directions and class standards, as well as interacting with peers. However, her self-care, interactions with staff, coping with frustration, attendance, and punctuality were considered average. Testing observations noted Emma Rose was cooperative and able to complete all tasks presented. At that time, SAI services were provided for 240 minutes weekly in a resource setting, and short-term counseling continued to support self-regulation. Information on early development confirmed milestone attainment except for delays in walking and talking.

blocks.prose: Emma Rose Callahan is currently enrolled at Ridgeway High School, having transitioned from specialized instruction in English and Study Skills at FHS, and previously attended home-based education through Options for Youth. She describes the effect of her medication as significant for daily functioning, stating, “Without meds it’s really hard, with meds it’s fine.” Emma Rose self-reports a history of tonsillectomy, which resolved previous sleep apnea. She is preparing for Math 1 using packets and acknowledges difficulty and lack of confidence in math. When describing her writing, she expresses enjoyment of using metaphors and has written essays on philosophical topics such as life and death. Persistence and effort are notable characteristics; she describes working slowly and carefully, rehearsing repeated listening to get words correct in reading. Emma Rose identifies public speaking as a potential area of strength. During discussion, her tone is flat when reading aloud but otherwise her conversational pace is normal. Interactions during assessment revealed a quiet demeanor, with intermittent eye contact; she demonstrated cooperation and persistence, occasionally expressing frustration but able to laugh at herself. Attention and concentration are described as cautious, with occasional impulsivity; she often self-corrects but makes errors at times due to poor attention. She reports average stamina, but notes that she is typically self-directed and works hard despite a dislike of math.

At the time of the current assessment, Emma Rose is a ninth-grade student at Ridgeway High School. Her mother confirms an active IEP for specific learning disability and related services, including Specialized Academic Instruction in math and study skills, with additional support for career and college awareness. Academic weaknesses are consistently noted in math fluency/numerical operations and written expression, while transition skills also remain a goal area. Her math diagnostic places her at the 18th percentile nationally, and math scores across content areas remain low. Emma Rose is reading at a seventh-grade level and demonstrates above standard performance in writing and research, though she received a 15/25 on a recent vocabulary quiz. Written language remains an area of need, as reflected in writing samples and IEP goals for expository essays. In her classes, Emma Rose is described as polite, engaged, and hard-working, helping peers and taking her classwork seriously. She has also demonstrated progress in math support, with recent assessment scores around 86%. Attendance is good and there are no behaviors interfering with learning; however, her shyness limits her willingness to seek help. Motivation is variable, and she is reported to sometimes have difficulty staying awake during morning classes, likely related to ongoing sleep issues; adjustments such as taking breaks and drinking water are being used. Medical history includes a diagnosis of hypothyroidism (with medication being adjusted), ADHD, and RAD, as well as seasonal allergies. At present, her mother reports no need for a health plan, but Emma Rose is being fitted for a CPAP machine and will participate in a sleep study. Her IEP team has approved an alternative pathway to a diploma (California Alternative Assessment), with anticipated completion by 2028. There are no concerns regarding vision, hearing, or access to curriculum through assistive technology, and Emma Rose receives instruction in a structured English immersion/multilingual setting.

Emma Rose's mother adds that in early childhood, sensory sensitivities (e.g., noise and touch) and a diagnosis of ADHD were present. Sleep problems and seasonal allergies have been longstanding issues. Early behavior rating scales reflected very elevated scores in depression and clinically significant home-based behaviors included inattention, aggression/defiance, struggles with peer relations, and executive functioning deficits. The home setting continues to see challenges with organization, attention regulation, and emotional reactivity, though recent school reports do not describe interfering behaviors.

Mr. Hollis, a teacher at Ridgeway High, reports that Emma Rose shows capacity in both written and applied academic tasks; for example, she is able to locate health-related articles and write summaries about them. Teachers overall describe her as polite, engaged, and motivated, with a willingness to support classmates. She has made progress in Math support classes, is generally a pleasure to have in class, and demonstrates best-effort work on assigned tasks.

Previous assessments and parent interviews identified several areas of clinical concern: ongoing behavior symptoms associated with aggression, conduct problems, atypical behaviors, and adaptive skills were noted, as well as executive functioning deficits, defiance/aggression, and difficulties with peer relations. Parent-completed rating scales showed very elevated scores in depressive symptoms (both emotional and functional composites). Concerns were also endorsed regarding depression, somatization, and attention problems, consistent across home and school reports.

Combined parent and teacher feedback continues to reflect clinically significant levels of inattention, depression, somatic complaints, and attention problems in both settings. Mrs. Reed, a former classroom teacher, noted additional concerns including withdrawal, learning problems, and peer relations. Hyperactive symptoms have not been observed at school.

Teachers at various stages report that, while Emma Rose continues to demonstrate areas of need—particularly in attention, following directions, sustaining peer relationships, and written expression—she also demonstrates average abilities in communication, motor skills, adaptive daily living, and general academic participation. Behavioral observations in the school setting highlight her shyness and tendency to avoid seeking help but do not identify disruptive behavior that would impede learning.
